en: Salutations to the venerable gurus.
Herein lies the *Smṛtimuktāvalī* compiled by Kṛṣṇācārya.
I worship that Hari, for whose pleasure dharma— proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti— is well-practiced, and who is the cause of perfect knowledge, liberation, and the like.
I worship my own Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is accompanied by jewels among women such as Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā, and who bestows all desired objects.
I worship the venerable Ānandatīrtha, the sage Jayatīrtha,
and my gurus beginning with Vyāsatīrtha, Jayendratīrtha, and Sudhīndra.
I perpetually revere my teachers of learning, the venerable Raghavendra Gurus, who are lions among wicked disputants and the propagators of the Madhva scriptures.
The *Smṛtimuktāvalī*, a neck-ornament for the learned,
is composed by the scholar Kṛṣṇācārya for the delight of virtuous people.
The conduct of the illustrious Madhva school is entirely virtuous, rooted in the Smṛtis;
indeed, it is the most excellent of all good practices—so firmly held by those of dull vision.
In order to generate confidence and for the easy understanding of great-souled ones,
the Smṛtis were compiled in ancient times by high-minded and disciplined sages.
Even from that, I shall extract [the essence] for the easy understanding of those of small intellect;
may Hari, well-pleased by this investigation of the Dharmaśāstra, grant the fruit [of my labor].
O venerable teacher, because of you, this labor of mine has become fruitful;
for I do not understand the meaning of any word or the meaning of any sentence anywhere.
May the virtuous show compassion merely by taking this into memory.
Regarding the determination that actions must be performed:

here, since the liberation desired by everyone—expressed as "May there be happiness for me, and may even the slightest suffering not occur"—does not arise without direct realization of the Lord; and since that realization is not possible without hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; and since those are not possible without the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*); and since that purification is not possible without the performance of virtuous actions (*sat-karma*) as prescribed in the *Smṛtis*; therefore, it has been established by all that one must perform virtuous actions according to the method taught in the *Smṛtis* in order to attain the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation through this successive sequence.

Regarding this, Manu says: "One should constantly perform, without laziness, one's own duty as ordained by the Veda; for performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. And: "A human being who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti obtains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. And regarding the necessity of possessing good conduct, Vyāsa says: "Even if he is devoid of Vedic study, a Brāhmaṇa who is faithful, has conquered his senses, and is endowed with good conduct shall attain a meritorious state."

Viṣṇu states the fault incurred by failing to perform these duties: "Whatever injunctions there may be, whether Śrauta or Smārta, all must be performed with devotion by those living in the household; otherwise, one incurs sin. Saṃvarta says: "Through good conduct, one attains the state of a deity as well as that of a ṛṣi; in its opposite, one attains birth in a base womb or as a human. And in the Gītā: "He who, casting aside the ordinance of the scriptures, acts under the impulse of desire, attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal."

Vyāsa states: "He who, out of atheism or laziness, does not perform what is declared in the scriptures, goes to terrible hells and is born among the animal species. In the *Pramāṇasaṅgraha*: "That twice-born one who does not practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti should be known as a heretic (pāṣaṇḍin), despised in all the worlds. Thus it is said. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "By transgressing the conduct of the virtuous, no one attains prosperity," so said the Blessed Lord Aurva to the inquiring Maitreya, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that ritual actions must be performed according to the methods declared in the Smṛtis and other such sources.

And these are the authorities for the fact that those actions, when performed without desire for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, are the cause of one’s own goal. "Niṣkāma" means being devoid of the intention for any other fruit. Yājñavalkya says: "O Gārgī, liberation stands in the hand of him who performs what is prescribed for his caste and stage of life according to the injunctions, free from desire, and in accordance with the rules."

"Every day, for all four social classes (*varṇas*), the duty prescribed by the injunctions must be performed, free from the intention of desire. The fault in performing actions preceded by desire is stated in that very same place: "Gārgī, when the very duty prescribed for a class and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) is performed with a motive of gain or preceded by desire, bondage stands ready in one's hand," and so forth. Regarding the point that these duties should be performed for the sake of pleasing Hari, [it is said]: "There is no other path to liberation than the rule of the stages of life as described."

"Therefore, one should perform actions for the satisfaction of the Supreme Self," so says Vyāsa. Also in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Whatever activities of embodied beings proceed from their own nature beginning at dawn, by offering those to Viṣṇu, one is liberated from the bonds of karma. In the Gītā: "By worshipping Him through one's own duty—He from whom the activity of all beings proceeds and by whom all this is pervaded—a human being attains perfection. And in the Bhāgavata: "With body, speech, mind, and senses," and so forth.

Hārīta says: "Therefore, O best of kings, resorting to supreme devotion as a servant, one should always perform obligatory and occasional rites for the constant pleasure of Hari. Charity, austerity, and sacrifice—these three types of action are proclaimed; all of these one should perform with a well-composed mind solely for the pleasure of the Blessed Lord. Śāṇḍilya says: "The Blessed Lord alone is to be propitiated through the eternal Vedic duties, both those characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) and those characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtta*), which grant both heaven and liberation."

"He alone is to be worshipped in every way, for there is no other who delivers one from saṃsāra; the Lord, the Master, is to be propitiated by both knowledge and action. Thus says Aurva: "The student, the householder, the mendicant, and likewise the forest-dweller—performing their own respective duties, they worship Viṣṇu alone. Directing the fire-ritual, recitation, bathing, austerity, and even Vedic study toward Him alone, the Lord of Gods, perform [these] daily without sloth. Hārīta says: "One should always worship Him alone and indeed offer salutations to Him alone."

Having meditated, one should mutter [the mantra] to that very Lord; one should cause Him alone to hear the Veda. One should perform vows, fasts, and observances directed toward Him alone. One should be one whose enjoyments are dedicated to Him through the consumption of food, drink, and so forth. There should never be attachment to one's own interests or one's own wife, nor to anything else. Thus it is said. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "By a person who follows the conduct of his caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that causes Him satisfaction."

In the *Vāyupurāṇa* as well: "The Lord Viṣṇu created the place, the time, and the rituals for the sake of service; therefore, one should worship Him incessantly. Having thus resolved and arisen, one should commence all actions [with this thought]: "I shall do, I shall eat, I shall offer oblations, and I shall give, all for the sake of Viṣṇu; never for my own sake," so should the man performing action speak at any time. In the *Gītā*: "Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, and whatever you give..."

"What you perform as austerity, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me" (Gītā 18.46). Also, in the *Bhāgavata*: "Even inaction is devoid of devotion to Acyuta," and so forth; and in the *Gītā*: "From whom proceeds the activity of all beings," and "Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind fixed on the Supreme Self," and so forth. Furthermore, because of such passages as "in which action becomes inexhaustible" and "in which all actions [are offered]," the Teachers have stated this very intention in the *Smṛtis* on Right Conduct (*Sadācāra*) and elsewhere.

And in the *Kṛṣṇāmṛtamahārṇava*: "Vedic action is twofold: active (*pravṛtta*) and withdrawn (*nivṛtta*). By both of these, that Puruṣa, who is the embodiment of all, is worshipped. Indeed, he is worshipped by means of the paths of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas through active rites—he who is the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice, the Puruṣa, the Supreme Puruṣa. He, whose self is knowledge and whose form is knowledge, is worshipped by means of the yoga of knowledge on the path of withdrawal by yogis; [therein] Viṣṇu is the bestower of the fruit of liberation. Thus it is said.

Regarding the sin incurred by performing actions without dedicating them to Him, Hārīta says: "The man who performs action without dedicating it to the Blessed One should be known as a heretic (pāṣaṇḍī), despised in all the worlds. Even after sacrificing with hundreds of Aśvamedhas or hundreds of Vājapeyas, those who have their backs turned to Nārāyaṇa do not attain a good state. Also in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Whether one is a practitioner of penance or devoted to all duties, without offering [the fruit] to Him, one undoubtedly does not obtain the full result."

In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* as well: "They say that sacrifice, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth, as prescribed in the Vedas, when performed with Keśava as the intended object, are *dharma*; but that very same act is *adharma* if it is displeasing to Hari. In another place in that same work: "Those ritual acts such as sacrifices which are indeed declared in the Vedas, if they are performed while considering them to be for the sake of the Supreme Deity, they shall be auspicious; otherwise, they are indeed fruitless. And in the *Bhāgavata*: "Ascetics, those devoted to charity, those possessed of fame, those of noble mind, those who know the mantras, and those who are most auspicious..."

"Salutations again and again to Him of auspicious renown, by surrendering to whom they find security. Thus ends the *Śuka-stuti*. For fear of excessive length, I shall desist from further citation. In this manner, actions performed for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu yield the fruit of liberation according to the method previously described. As it is said in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "For actions such as renunciation lead to the direct vision of the Lord; and the direct vision of the Lord seeks nothing at all for the sake of liberation."

Having placed all of that within it, [action] becomes the means for liberation. And in the Gītā: "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge," and "By action one spreads knowledge; by knowledge one becomes immortal," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that actions must be performed for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, in order to attain the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation.

If it is objected that, since all actions thus have the propitiation of Viṣṇu as their fruit, sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Citrā would not have heaven, cattle, and so forth as their fruits—because one cause cannot produce a different effect—it is replied: even though actions like the Jyotiṣṭoma have heaven and the like as their fruits, the propitiation of Hari exists as their means; and since it functions as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), there is no contradiction in its producing both effects, namely the primary fruit and the intermediate result.

And it is accepted by all that a single sacrifice possesses the power to produce both such an *apūrva* (unseen potency) and heaven. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for the *Śrīmad-Bhāṣya* states: "By action, the lowest grace (*prasāda*) is said to be attained; by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, the middling; and the highest grace is considered to be through the perfection of knowledge. From the lowest grace of Viṣṇu, the world of heaven (*svargaloka*) is proclaimed; from the middling, Janaloka and the others; but the highest indeed bestows liberation. Thus, in the *Śrīmad-Bhāṣya*.

And in the *Bhāradvāja-saṃhitā* it is said: "The lowest [devotee] is born through ritual action (*karman*), the middling through hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, and the highest through the perfection of knowledge; such is the grace of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu). From the lowest grace of Viṣṇu, the heavenly world is proclaimed. Because of such statements, or alternatively, even if both [liberation and worldly results] are independent means, there is no contradiction regarding sacrifices and the like, since—just as the constant use of *khadira* wood for the sake of vigor (*vīrya*) can serve both purposes—it is possible for this [sacrifice] to serve both purposes. Nor is there a contradiction between what has been enjoined and what is being enjoined.

Just as the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā" is employed in the Śrauta Āgneya sacrifice and in Smārta rites such as the recitation and oblation to Aṅgāraka, and likewise the mantra "Āpyāyasva" is employed in the Saumya Patnīsaṃyāja and for the swelling of the Soma juice, so too here, since there is no contradiction between the two statements and it is logical that [the Lord] is the cause of both, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Thus it is said in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O child, by worshipping me, a person attains liberation without delay; with the mind dedicated to me, what need is there to mention fruits such as heaven?"

In another place in that very same work: "O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, even the status of Indra is an obstacle [to liberation]. And in the *Bhāgavata*: "What is unattainable when the Blessed One, the abode of Śrī, is pleased? and so on. Also in the *Brāhma*: "For He alone is the supreme Person, the giver of fruits to all; there is no other who is either the enjoyer of actions or the giver of their fruit," and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that by stating that all rites must be performed with Viṣṇu as the object, there would follow the consequence that Viṣṇu is the deity for every single rite, which would result in the collapse of the established distinction between rites dedicated to a single deity and those dedicated to two deities; [and] if in cases such as "an eleven-potherd offering for Indra" (aindram ekādaśakapālam), Indra and others alone were the deities—[we reply: rather, it is Viṣṇu qualified by that [deity] who is the deity, and this fact is established by grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), wherein the deity-suffix (*devatātaddhita*) heard after each respective nominal stem (*prātipadika*) conveys that the deityhood belongs to the meaning of that stem—as in the case of "belonging to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇam*).

In passages such as "the oblation made of barley is for Rudra," and so forth; likewise, in the present case as well, by means of the deity-designating secondary suffix (taddhita) heard following the words "Indra" and so on, Viṣṇu qualified as Purandara and others possesses the status of the deity, because it is precisely such [a qualified being] that constitutes the meaning of the nominal stems "Indra" and so forth.

That Viṣṇu is the primary referent (*prātipadikārtha*) of words such as "Indra" is understood from such scriptural passages as, "He who alone is the bestower of names among the gods," and "Into whom all names enter," as well as from the statements of the Teacher (Madhva): "Janārdana alone is primarily denoted by all words. Alternatively, the justification lies in their relationship as subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), as expressed in such texts as, "The deities act like a cloak [for Him]. And in the *Tantra-bhāgavata*: "By action that is independent and offered to Viṣṇu alone..."

"Right knowledge shall arise for men preceded by the satisfaction of the deities. Through the instruction [of the Lord], all the deities become satisfied in the Blessed One alone; because they are instructed as being His limbs, they attain satisfaction in Him. When those lords of the gods and Viṣṇu are satisfied, supreme knowledge arises; through that very [knowledge], you shall attain perfection and be liberated from the bondage of karma. Thus it is said. Also in the Bhāgavata: "Some twice-born performers of Vedic sacrifices worship You through the triple Vedic science..."

“They worship with various sacrifices under the name of the goddesses of manifold forms. Thus it is said. Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: “Hari, who desires heaven, eats the oblation offered through your mouth; likewise, Janārdana himself eats [the offering] from those seeking liberation. For he alone is the Supreme Person, the giver of fruit to all; there is no other who is the enjoyer of actions or the giver of their fruit. Those who, out of independence, perform the great rites prescribed by the Veda...”

"Indeed, those who perform sacrifices for deities without the pleasure of the Blessed Lord are considered heretics (pāṣaṇḍinaḥ), even if they offer oblations and give gifts with reference to Him, provided they do not know Hari, the Acyuta, the enjoyer of all sacrifices; such a person is to be known as a heretic, being independent in his ritual acts. Therefore, it is established that since Viṣṇu—who is superior to Purandara and others—is the referent of terms such as Indra, it is not illogical for Him to be the ultimate object of all ritual actions.
All of this is well-known from the *Tattvaprakāśikā* commentary on the *Anumānika-Adhikaraṇa*. I shall desist here for fear of prolixity.

In this context, the evidence for the position that those actions must be performed even by one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*) is stated as follows: there is the Śruti, "Having obtained knowledge from the teacher, one should behold this Self; he should become tranquil, he should become self-controlled"; and there is the Smṛti cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna* and other sources, such as: "Even while beholding his own Self, Indra performed ritual action without ceasing; for ten million years he drank smoke with extreme suffering, and for ten thousand years the Sun performed penance with his head hanging downwards."

Nor is there any dispute regarding their status as knowers of reality (*tattvajñānin*), for the *Smṛti* cited in the *Gītā-tātparya* states: "Those who have not attained the vision of Brahman do not reach the state of the gods," and so forth. Furthermore, since deities also possess the desire for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) and the like, their eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) has been properly explained in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* section of the *Bhāṣya* and other works, beginning with the sūtra: "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that they are eligible] even above that, because it is possible. Moreover, the eligibility of the gods for ritual action is seen repeatedly in the *Śrutis*.

For instance, there are such scriptural passages as: "By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice"; "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (satra)"; "The gods indeed performed the sacrifice"; "The gods indeed performed the sacrifice by means of the Caturhotṛ formulas"; "When the Viśvedevas sacrificed together"; "Indra performed a hundred horse-sacrifices (aśvamedha)"; and "The gods caused Varuṇa to sacrifice," and so forth. Thereafter, all the deities, Brahmā, and the great seers (maharṣis) performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.

And so on, according to [the authority of] Smṛti. Nor is there futility for actions performed after the attainment of knowledge due to the absence of fruit; for even so, as stated in the Kauṇḍaravya-Śruti: "In whatever manner one performs action, in that same manner one becomes greater," and in the Smṛti cited in the Bhāṣya: "Everything is attained through knowledge alone, but through action one may become superior; even among the gods who possess knowledge, distinction arises through actions. This is because such texts describe the increase of bliss and other such results as the fruit of those actions.

Nor is there a lack of authoritative evidence for this, for the Śruti states: "This is the inquiry into bliss," and so forth; and the Padma Purāṇa says: "From the kings up to the Lord of a Hundred Worlds (Śatadhṛti), those who have attained liberation rejoice with all their qualities increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage. Furthermore, it is stated in the Bhāgavata and other texts: "Among even the liberated and perfected ones, one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa with a tranquil self is very difficult to find," and so on. [These citations] are not written out here for fear of prolixity. Therefore, it is established that ritual actions must be performed by both those who know the Truth and by the gods.

Regarding the *Smṛtis* and so forth, as well as their authors: since the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, *Pañcarātra-saṃhitās*, and the treatises composed by Manu and others are themselves authoritative regarding the Dharma expounded in this work, their authors and those *Purāṇas* (and *Saṃhitās*) are first examined. In that regard, Yājñavalkya states: "Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama."

"Śātātapa and Vasiṣṭha are the originators (promulgators) of the Dharmaśāstras. Thus [says] Paiṭhīnasi: "Among them are Manu, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Atri, Uśanas, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Guru, Pracetas, Nārada, the Yogin, Bodhāyana, Pitāmaha, Sumantu, Kāśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīna, Vyāghra, Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgi, and likewise Kārṣṇājini."

Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Jātūkarṇya, Kapiñjala, Bodhāyana, Kaṇāda, Viśvāmitra, Paiṭhīnasi, and Gobhila are the authors of the Upasmṛtis. Furthermore, the Purāṇas are enumerated in the Padma Purāṇa as follows: the Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Bhāgavata; likewise the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh; the Āgneya is declared the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is remembered as the ninth.

The tenth is the Brahmavaivarta; the eleventh is remembered as the Laiṅga; the twelfth is declared to be the Vāmana; the thirteenth is the Vārāha; the fourteenth is declared to be the Mātsya; the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma; the sixteenth is declared to be the Gāruḍa; the seventeenth is remembered as the Skānda; and the eighteenth is the Brahmāṇḍa—these are the Purāṇas in their proper order. Furthermore, there are the Vāyavya, Bhārgava, Soma, Brahmāṇḍa, and likewise the Kauśika.

The Parāśara, Nāradīya, Nārasiṃha, Kāpila, Vāsiṣṭha, Śivadharma, Mārīca, Mānava, Skānda, Durvāsas, Āditya, Vāruṇa, and Śāmbara—these are declared to be the eighteen Upapurāṇas. The Mahābhārata is the Itihāsa. These Smṛtis and Purāṇas are of three kinds, according to the division of Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa. Among them, only the Sāttvika ones are to be accepted, as they have liberation as their fruit.

The others, which have heaven and hell as their fruits, are stated in the forty-second chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Pādma Purāṇa, in the dialogue with Maheśvara: "O lady of auspicious appearance! Know that the Vaiṣṇava, Nāradīya, the auspicious Bhāgavata, Gāruḍa, Pādma, and Vārāha are Sāttvika Purāṇas. Furthermore, know from me that the Brahmāṇḍa, Brahmavaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya, Bhaviṣya, Vāmana, and Brāhma are Rājasa."

"Know from me that these six—the Mātsya, Kaurma, Laiṅga, Śaiva, Skānda, and likewise the Āgneya—are tāmasa. The sāttvika ones are said to bestow liberation; the auspicious rājasa ones bestow heaven; and likewise, O Goddess, the tāmasa ones are the causes for attaining hell. Thus it is said. In the same way, the Smṛtis are also mentioned in that very place: "Likewise, O lady of auspicious vision, the Smṛtis have been proclaimed by the sages endowed with the three guṇas as sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa."

The Vāsiṣṭha, Hārīta, Vyāsa, Parāśara, Bhāradvāja, and Kāśyapa are the Sāttvika codes; they are auspicious and bestow liberation. The Mānava, Yājñavalkya, Ātreya, Dākṣa, Kātyāyana, and Vaiṣṇava are the Rājasa codes; they are auspicious and grant heaven. The Gautama, Bārhaspatya, Sāṃvarta, and the Yama-smṛti, as well as the Śāṅkha and Aiśānasa, O Goddess, are the Tāmasa codes; they lead to hell.

The fact that those belonging to the *tāmasa* category are to be abandoned is stated in that very same place: "What is the use of saying much more here? Whether in the Purāṇas or even in the Smṛtis, the wise man should avoid those *tāmasa* [works], for they lead only to hell. [Objection: But if the *tāmasa* Smṛtis and Purāṇas are not to be accepted, how can the words spoken therein be cited as authoritative corroboration? [Reply: It is not so; for it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa* itself: "That which is found even in the Śiva-śāstra should be accepted if it is consistent with the teachings of the Lord (the Bhagavat-śāstra), as was respectfully told by Śiva himself to Ṣaṇmukha."

It should not be argued that the *Tātparya-nirṇaya* states, "Whatever among these is not contradictory [to our own system], that which has been stated therein is not to be rejected," and thus even within the *tāmasa* (dark) scriptures, the non-contradictory portions are to be accepted. For by that statement, although the non-contradictory portions regarding the Lord’s teachings (*bhagavac-chāstra*) within the *tāmasa* works are to be accepted, there would be no basis for accepting those statements concerning the parts relating to duties to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-karma-bhāga*). If it is asked why this is so, the answer is: because there is no supporting factor; whereas within the *tāmasa* works, the *sāttvika* (pure) portions must be adopted because they conform to the *sāttvika* scriptures.

Since there is no regulating factor other than conformity [to scripture] even for the acceptance of that which is superior to the Blessed One, thus concludes the determination regarding the authors of the Smṛtis and the Purāṇas.
The true nature of *dharma* and its definition.

Now, if it is asked what kind of thing this *dharma* is—the authority of which regarding its own subject matter has been asserted in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth—it is replied: because Jaimini stated that "dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by *codanā*," and because Jaimini also stated that "dharma is indeed that which is enjoined by the Veda, while adharma is its opposite," and because it is likewise stated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* that "dharma is indeed that which is enjoined by the Veda, while adharma is its opposite," its definition is simply being cognizable through *codanā* while being a beneficial purpose (*artha*).

Nor is there a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding those [duties] rooted in custom (ācāra), because even there exists the quality of being knowable through an injunction (codanā) inferred from a Smṛti which itself is inferred from custom. As it has been said: "Having known the Smṛti from custom, one then postulates a Śruti from the Smṛti. On this point, Manu also says: "That which is practiced by the learned, the virtuous, and those always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart—that one should determine to be Dharma."

The meaning of this is as follows: that which is "constantly practiced by the wise" means it is perpetually performed as a duty (*dharma*), and not occasionally due to motives such as grief or delusion. Furthermore, it is "approved by the heart," meaning it is accepted with natural inclination as the very means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), and not out of anger. One should determine that such a matter is *dharma*. Viśvāmitra also said: "That which the noble ones who know the scriptures praise while it is being performed..."

"That which they praise is Dharma; that which they censure is declared to be Adharma. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya specifically states the characteristics of Dharma: "That which is given to a worthy recipient (pātra) at the proper place and time, by the right means, with a substance endowed with faith—that is the complete definition of Dharma. Furthermore: "The first Dharma is that declared in the Vedas, another is that [declared] in the Dharmaśāstra, and the third is the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra); such is the threefold definition of Dharma."

In another Smṛti as well: "Massaging one who is weary on the road, clearing away the remnants of food from twice-born men, and following the path of the Vedas—this is the threefold definition of Dharma. In the Skanda Purāṇa also: "Truthful speech, the gift of water for the feet, keeping a vigil on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), and the protection of those dependent on one—this is the fourfold essence of Dharma. "Charity toward the destitute, the performance of rites for Viṣṇu, the avoidance of what is forbidden, and honoring those of virtuous conduct—Dharma is recorded as being fivefold."

"The gift of a bed, delight in the Dharma, the recitation of the Mahābhārata, and the life-story of Raghunātha destroy even great sins. "Bathing with *dhātrī* fruit, beneficial speech, the study of the Vedas, stories of Hari, eating alms-food, and the worship of the guru—this is the sixfold definition of Dharma. In another Smṛti: "Giving to a worthy recipient, devotion to Kṛṣṇa, honoring one's mother and father, speaking words of love, and offering a morsel of grass to a cow—this is the sixfold definition of Dharma."

Yājñavalkya says: "Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the definition of Dharma. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is steadfastness. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the absence of mental agitation even when wronged. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the mind. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the refusal to take what is not given. Purity (*śauca*) is both external and internal. Control of the senses (*indriyanigraha*) is the turning back of the senses from forbidden objects. Modesty (*hrī*) is the desisting from improper actions. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*).

Truth (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to reality; and that should be understood as being only what is pleasant. Thus Manu says: "One should speak the truth, one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal law (*sanātana-dharma*). Freedom from anger (*akrodha*) is the absence of wrath. The meaning is that this decad (the group of ten) constitutes the definition of *dharma*. Bṛhaspati mentions other attributes of *dharma*: "Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness..."

Freedom from miserliness and freedom from covetousness are common to all [virtues]. He himself described their essential nature: "Whether toward others, one's circle of kinsmen, a friend, or an enemy, one must always protect those who have fallen into distress; this is proclaimed as compassion (dayā). When external or internal suffering arises at any time, not becoming angry and not striking back—this is proclaimed as forbearance (kṣamā). Not destroying the virtues of the virtuous, praising even those with meager virtues, and not taking pleasure in the faults of others—this is proclaimed as freedom from malice (anasūyā)."

Avoidance of forbidden food, association with blameless persons, and steadfastness in one’s own duty—this is proclaimed as purity. That action which causes the body to suffer, even if it be a very auspicious deed, must not be performed excessively; that is called lack of exertion. Constant practice of what is commendable and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared to be auspicious by the seers who perceive the truth. One should give even from a little, with a heart free from dejection.

"Whatever is done day by day without miserliness is indeed remembered as such. One should be content with whatever small thing arises; not considering the wealth of another, that is proclaimed as freedom from longing."

Now, regarding the distinctions among dharmas: in the *Mahābhārata* it is said— "Dharma in this world is manifold, arising from the various openings of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*). Local customs (*deśadharma*) are observed, as are family customs (*kuladharma*), O beautiful one! There are also duties pertaining to caste (*jātidharma*), duties pertaining to age (*vayodharma*), duties pertaining to qualities (*guṇadharma*), duties pertaining to the body and time (*śarīrakāladharma*), and likewise duties pertaining to times of distress (*āpaddharma*). This diversity of dharma is established by the inhabitants of the world. Sumantu also says: "That dharma which proceeds by relying upon the single status of being a social class (*varṇatva*)," [is called *varṇadharma*].

That which is prescribed according to the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is indeed called the duty of caste (varṇadharma). That authority which proceeds by relying upon a stage of life (āśrama) is the duty of that stage of life, such as the practice of begging for alms and so forth, as enjoined. That which proceeds by taking both caste and stage of life as its basis is the duty of caste and stage of life (varṇāśramadharma), such as the girdle of muñja grass (mauñjī) worn by a student. That which proceeds by virtue of a particular quality (guṇa) is called the duty of quality (guṇadharma), such as the protection of subjects by one who has been consecrated as a king (mūrdhābhiṣikta).
"That dharma which proceeds by depending upon a single cause is to be known as 'caused' (naimittika), just like the rule for penance. Thus ends the definition of dharma.

Regarding the authorities on Dharma, there are indeed authorities on Dharma. On this point, Yājñavalkya states: "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vedāṅgas—these fourteen, together with the Vedas, are the seats of knowledge and of Dharma. In the Aparārka commentary: "Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—these three, along with Arthaśāstra as the fourth; these are remembered as the eighteen branches of learning (vidyā). And Yājñavalkya says: "The Śruti, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to one’s own self."

"Desire born of right resolve is remembered as this very root of Dharma. Thus says Manu: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the Smṛtis and the conduct (śīla) of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous (sādhus), and also self-satisfaction (ātmanastuṣṭi). Self-satisfaction refers to that pleasure which arises in one’s own mind when performing among optional matters; that too is an authority. 'Virtuous ones' refers to the cultured (śiṣṭas). And so Manu says: 'The conduct of the cultured, the Smṛtis, and the Vedas—this is the threefold characteristic of Dharma. 'Characteristic' means authority (pramāṇa)."

He (Bṛhaspati) also stated the definition of a cultured person (*śiṣṭa*): "Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been mastered through righteous means—those Brāhmaṇas are to be known as *śiṣṭas*, for they are the authorities for the direct perception of the Śruti. The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the supplements of the Veda. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'This man will lead me astray.'"

Baudhāyana says: "The cultured (śiṣṭas) are indeed free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing grain in jars [and other limited stores], free from greed, and bereft of hypocrisy, pride, avarice, delusion, intoxication, and anger. Likewise, in the Araṇyaparvan: "Those who do not become angry, who do not find fault in others, who are free from egoism and envy, upright, endowed with tranquility—they are the ones whose conduct is that of the cultured. Those who are advanced in the three Vedas, pure, intelligent, renowned, devoted to service of their gurus, and self-controlled—they are the ones whose conduct is that of the cultured. Thus it is said.

Hārīta also says: "The virtuous (sādhu) are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word 'sat' denotes the virtuous. That which is their conduct is called *sadācāra* (the conduct of the good). Regarding the statement "the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is authoritative," the conduct of the gods and others should not be emulated, because of the scriptural mention of sin (*pratyavāya*). As Manu says: "A transgression of dharma is seen among the great, as well as acts of rashness. Observing that, the inferior and weak man who practices [those acts] perishes. The splendor, strength, bodies, and senses of the ancients [were different]."

"They are not defiled by defects, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. Thus says Bodhāyana: "That which has been performed by the gods and that which has been performed by the sages—though it may not be [ordinarily] to be performed by humans—one should perform such an action when it is so prescribed. Thus says Aṅgiras: "One who desires the accomplishment of dharma should perform what is enjoined by that triad: perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions."

Furthermore, Manu states that where there are no direct scriptural injunctions (*śruti*) and so forth, the word of the assembly (*pariṣad*) is the authority: "If it be asked how it should be regarding duties not mentioned in the tradition, whatever learned (*śiṣṭa*) Brāhmaṇas declare shall be the duty, free from doubt. Here, "regarding duties" means regarding the authorities for determining duty. Those learned ones must also consist of at least ten members. To this effect, Gautama says: "In the case of what is not mentioned in the tradition, an act praised by at least ten learned men who possess the power of reasoning (*ūhavat*) should be performed."

The meaning is that what has been declared as "praiseworthy" by those who have restrained themselves must be performed. Manu also says: "One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and one who knows the Sāmaveda—these three at minimum are to be known as an assembly for the resolution of doubts regarding Dharma. Or, even a single person who is preeminent in the knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) and knows the Dharma, whatever matter he declares to be consistent with Dharma, that too shall be Dharma.

Hārīta states that even the words of an assembly are to be accepted only if they follow the Vedas: "The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative; speech endowed with righteousness and purpose is authoritative. For one for whom authority does not exist as authority, who would make his word authoritative? "Who should establish the rules of dharma when there is conflict? One who knows logic, understands the Dharmaśāstras, and is a rationalist is considered fit for the assembly. [But this does not apply to] those who do not observe vows, who have not studied the mantras, and who subsist merely by the name of their caste."

"A multitude gathered by the thousands does not constitute an assembly [of authority]. Whatever expiation for sins those three who know the Vedas may prescribe shall serve for their purification; for the word of the learned is indeed purifying. This refers to cases of minor offenses. Furthermore, the consensus of those who know the Dharma is also an authority in certain instances. Thus says Āpastamba: "The consensus of those who know the Dharma and the Vedas are authoritative. In some cases, established tradition (*sampradāya*) is also an authority. Regarding this, Manu says: "That path by which his ancestors have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone..."

Therefore, one should travel on the path of the virtuous; traveling by that path, one is not seen [by the wicked]. Tradition (*sampradāya*) is conduct inherited through the succession of one's own family. That too is an authority when there is a conflict with the scriptures (*śāstra*). O Bhārata, where the course of the scriptures differs regarding all ritual acts—just as there is a distinction between the *homa* offered after sunrise and that offered before sunrise—in whatever family a wise man practices the conduct handed down through tradition, that is more weighty, O mighty-armed one, even than what is declared in all the scriptures. This is because of the statement of Sumantu. Thus end the authorities on Dharma. This concludes the justification for the authority of the Smṛtis.

If it is asked, "By what means do the aforementioned Smṛtis and other texts possess authority? we reply: by virtue of being rooted in the Veda. Nor is their composition rendered useless on the grounds that they are rooted in it; for the composition of Smṛtis is fruitful, as it serves to facilitate easy comprehension and to collect together what is scattered, since Vedic words have meanings that are difficult to grasp. As Marīci has said: "Vedic words are difficult to understand, and all [of them] are scattered..."

"Those very [works] which have clear meanings are established as authoritative in the Smṛti-tantra. Thus, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the eighteen Sūtras of Baudhāyana and others possess equal authority. Here, in the case of a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone possesses greater force. Among Smṛtis themselves, when there is mutual contradiction, that which has no room for application (niravakāśa) sublates that which has room (sāvakāśa), and the weak is sublated by the strong. It should be understood that this greater force arises from being without room for application, from multiplicity, from corroboration by other means of knowledge, from being characterized by *sattva*, and so forth.
A detailed exposition is to be found in the *Candrikā* and the *Antarnaya*.

And those eighteen Sūtras are enumerated in the Āgniveśya-sūtra: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the enumeration of the Sūtras. Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Dākṣāyaṇa, Āgastya, Śākalya, Āśvalāyana, Śāmbarīya, and Kātyāyana—these are the nine prior Sūtras. Vaikhānasa, Śaunakīya, Bhāradvāja, Āgniveśya, Jaiminīya, Mādhulya, Mādhyandina, Kauṇḍinya, and Gautama—these are the nine subsequent Sūtras."

Thus, there are eighteen bodily sacraments (*saṃskāras*). And so says Manu: "The sages perceive the *Śruti* and likewise remember the *Smṛti*; therefore, both are authoritative, as they are established by means of valid knowledge on this earth. That man who, relying on dialectical treatises (*hetuśāstra*), would despise these two—he is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda, and he should be excluded by the virtuous."

Regarding the fact that these [works], such as the *Smṛtis*, are not to be rejected, Yama also states: "Those Dharmaśāstras which were indeed composed by them in ancient times—these are authoritative and must not be discarded on the basis of mere reasoning; he who would destroy them with reasoning sinks into blind darkness. Vasiṣṭha also says: "The invalidation of the Vedas, the reviling of the Āryas, and a lack of settled conduct in all matters—this is the destruction of the self."

Regarding the fact that the authority of Smṛti must indeed be upheld, Aṅgiras states: "Authorities must be diligently protected by those who know what constitutes authority; for authorities collapse when they are not established by means of authorities. Regarding the authority of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as being equal to the Vedas, the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa says: "The Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan [Vedas], as well as the Mūla-Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Pañcarātra—these are designated as 'Vedas. And those Purāṇas here which the wise know to be Vaiṣṇava..."

"The authority of these [scriptures] is intrinsic; nothing further needs to be deliberated here. Thus, after presenting the four Vedas, the Śruti also states: "The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the fifth. This concludes the demonstration of the authority of the Smṛtis.
The study of the Dharmaśāstra:

Now, the Dharmaśāstra must also be studied just like the Veda. Regarding this, Manu says: "Just as the study of the Veda, so too this Dharmaśāstra must be studied according to the prescribed authority by one desiring heaven. And Bṛhaspati states that this occurs immediately after the study of the Veda: "Having thus consecrated his son with the rites beginning with the tonsure (daṇḍa), the father should then teach him the Veda, and likewise the Śāstra of Manu and the others."

The same author states the fault of not studying: "For the Śruti and Smṛti are considered the supreme eyes of the Brāhmaṇas; one who is deprived of one is called one-eyed, and one who lacks both is proclaimed to be blind. And: "Having studied the four Vedas along with the six limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations, those devoid of the Smṛti do not shine, like a night without the moon. Yama describes the fruit of that study and the eligible candidates: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who studies this scripture..."

"He purifies all the ancestors here—seven preceding and seven succeeding generations. So says Manu as well: "A Brāhmaṇa of firm vows who studies this scripture is never tainted by the defects of action born of mind, speech, or body. This must be studied with effort by a learned Brāhmaṇa, and it should be correctly expounded to the learned, and not by anyone else. This [passage] is intended to exclude the Śūdra from eligibility, for Yama has stated: "The Śūdra has no eligibility in the Vedas nor in the Smṛtis."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state that the fruit of engaging in this study is both worldly activity and renunciation: "The Dharmaśāstras are like medicine for diseases; they are the remedy that turns back those who have entered upon wrong paths and whose senses and minds are agitated. Regarding the specific fruit of retaining them, Yama says: "By retaining the Dharmaśāstra—which is righteous, conducive to fame, long life, merit, and likewise heaven—one shall attain the world of Brahmā."

Thus [it is said]. Manu also says: "He purifies his lineage, seven ancestors and seven descendants; indeed, even he alone is worthy of this entire earth. This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect; this constantly brings fame; this is the supreme means for attaining the highest good. It is auspicious, conducive to fame, long life, merit, and bestows both heaven and liberation; it is like the retention of the Vedic scriptures, for it is the retention of the treatise on Dharma."
"He does not die childless, nor does he fall into financial distress; merely by grasping this scripture, he attains equality with the virtuous. Thus ends the fruit of studying the Smṛti.
The determination regarding a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti.

Now, the determination regarding a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti. On this point, Manu says: "Where there is a conflict between two Śrutis, both are remembered as Dharma; for both of them have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise. Where there is a conflict, that is, a mutual contradiction, between two Śrutis, in that case both Dharmas propounded by the Śrutis are valid, because those two Dharmas were also declared by Manu and other ancient authorities.

If it is argued that—just as when there is a conflict between two means of knowledge (*māna*), validity belongs to only one of them, so too it must be for two Vedic texts (*śruti*)—therefore it is incorrect to say that both are *dharma*, we reply: "For what Mīmāṃsaka would say that when two scriptures are in mutual conflict..."

The purport of Manu’s statement is that both dharmas propounded by the Śruti are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is impossible for one to be a valid authority while the other is not—given that total sublation is untenable—and because the validity of the other means of knowledge is justified through the shifting of the subject matter, or by difference in time, or by difference in the qualified person, or by difference in location, or by being intended as a restriction, or by having a secondary meaning, or by referring to another application, or by having a different underlying intention. Thus, both are established by authority.

Alternatively, let there be sublation (*bādha*) in cases of contradiction where one [source] possesses greater authority; however, where there is equality of strength, since there is no sublation, an option (*vikalpa*) is necessary. Therefore, Manu’s statement that "both are dharma" is intended to mean this. And thus, by the same logic, when there is mutual contradiction between two *smṛtis*, two *purāṇas*, or two customs (*ācāras*), both are indeed dharma. This concludes the determination regarding contradictions among the *śruti* and the others. [Now follow] the various rites proclaimed in the *śruti* and *smṛti*.

Now, as it arises in the course of discussion, the various types of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti are briefly described—some being primary rites (*pradhāna-karma*), some auxiliary rites (*aṅga-karma*), some secondary auxiliary rites (*upāṅga-karma*), some subordinate rites (*gauṇa-karma*), and some substitute rites (*pratinidhi-karma*). Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "Rites should be performed during the northern solstice (*udagayana*), during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), and on auspicious days (*puṇyāha*). One should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*), proceed from the east toward the north, and likewise conclude the rite in the same direction as it began."

"Likewise, the conclusion [of rites] for the ancestors occurs on the dark fortnight; wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and with the sacrificial cord over the left arm (apasavya), the conclusion is toward the south. In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, it is stated that there are six ancillaries to the principal rite: "These six are indeed the ancillaries of the rite being performed: inquiry into the Śruti and Smṛti, faith, association with the virtuous, devotion to the deity to be propitiated, renunciation of the sense of agency, and restraint—these four are the ancillaries to be accomplished through that [inquiry]."

"Awakening at the proper times and reflection according to one's capacity, as well as mental composure and purity—this is considered the primary set of limbs. It should be understood that this group of four limbs pertains to the action being performed. He [the same author] states other limbs as well: "Solely offering [the fruit] to Viṣṇu is the first; faith is the second; freedom from desire and the longing for the pleasure of Hari are the two eyes. He states the six subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas) as follows: "In the same way, those who know recognize these six subsidiary limbs."

"Rinsing the mouth, chewing the tooth-stick, as well as the ritual sipping for purification, bathing, putting on the garment, and seventhly, the application of the *puṇḍra*—one should understand these as the preliminary rites (*karma*); only thereafter should one perform the primary rite. Through this preliminary rite, the knowledge that is the means to liberation arises. Without this knowledge, even if many rites are performed by men, they neither increase [their merit] anywhere nor do they become deficient anywhere. Thus it is said.

Kātyāyana states the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by way of another method: "Having purified oneself through clarity of mind, truthful speech, austerity, and the act of bathing, and having performed the sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform the ritual action. These actions are to be performed prior to the principal rite. He states a specific rule regarding this: "In a case where a ritual action is prescribed but it is not stated which hand of the performer is to be used, the right hand should be understood as the one that brings the actions to completion."

Manu also says: "The left hand should be used for what is contemptible, and the right for what is not contemptible; all rites should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and in a clockwise direction. Kātyāyana states a specific rule: "In those rites such as recitation (japa) and oblation (homa) where no fixed direction is prescribed, three directions are declared: the eastern (aindrī), the northern (saumyā), and the north-eastern (aparājitā). The north-eastern direction is called *aparājitā*. He states another specific rule regarding different duties: "One may be seated, standing, or bent forward, provided there is no such restriction [regarding posture]."

"It should be performed while seated, neither by one who is bowing nor by one who is standing. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states another specific rule concerning dharma: "If one should perform an action otherwise than it was begun due to confusion regarding the procedure, one should repeat that very part from which it became otherwise. If, upon completion, one should realize, 'This was done by me incorrectly,' one should perform only that much again; there is no repetition of the entire rite. However, if the principal act itself is not performed, it must be performed again along with all its ancillaries."

However, if there is non-performance of its constituent part (*tadaṅga*), there is neither repetition nor the performance of another [rite]. Gārgya states a specific rule: "A Brahmin who, out of delusion, performs a Smārta rite or an Itihāsa rite while disregarding the Vedic rite, is not joined with merit. This refers to the case of one who is capable. Regarding the case of incapacity: "If one is unable to perform the Śrauta rite, one should perform the Smārta; if even the Smārta is impossible, one should finally perform some other conduct (*ācāra*)."

On this very point, Vyāsa says: "If one is unable to perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti, one should perform those prescribed by the Smṛti; if one is also unable to perform those, the wise man should adopt the conduct of the virtuous. Kātyāyana states that a rite not mentioned in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) should be adopted and performed after being brought over from another Smṛti, according to the principle of the section on other branches (śākhāntarādhikaraṇa): "That which is not mentioned in one's own branch, provided it is not contradictory to it, should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites."

Furthermore, it is said: "That which is not stated in one's own Tantra (ātmatantra) should be performed according to another's Tantra (pāratantrika). In the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*, regarding the excellence of time (*kāla*) and substance (*dravya*), the primacy of time alone is declared: "If the primary means of accomplishment cannot be obtained at the primary time, then between time and substance, which has primacy and which has secondary status? Relying upon the primary time, let even a secondary substance suffice; there should be no waiting for a secondary time merely because the primary substance is unavailable."

Pulastya states a specific rule regarding ritual action: "If an action is performed at the wrong time, it must be performed again once the proper time arrives; however, that which one performs after the time has passed should be declared as unperformed."

The inclusion of even the secondary time (*gauṇa*) therein is an exception (*apavāda*). However, when for some reason the primary time (*mukhya-kāla*) is exceeded, Kātyāyana says: "When it is impossible to perform the rite during the primary time, it must be performed even during the secondary time; here, the secondary time should also be of such a nature. The definition of the secondary time is stated in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*: "The secondary time for a preceding rite is that which follows its own [prescribed] time; the upcoming rite [serves as the limit], just like the interval of the primary time."

Some maintain that there is a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) for a previous rite; during these secondary times, one should perform the rite as enjoined. One should perform the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) according to the prescribed methods of atonement (*prāyaścitta*); however, if the expiation has not been performed, one should perform that [rite] during the secondary time. Indeed, rites prescribed for the day which have been omitted through negligence, one should cause to be performed until the first watch (*prahara*) of the night. The meaning of this is: the interval of time between the previous rite and the primary time of the upcoming rite is the secondary time (*gauṇa*).

Some, however, maintain that even the primary time for a future action may be considered a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*). When both the secondary and primary times have been transgressed, one should perform penance according to the methods prescribed in the rules on penance (*prāyaścitta-vidhi*). In that regard, regarding the secondary time for a ritual, one should perform the rite even without having performed the penance. A specific detail is shown here in the *Saṅgraha*: "One should perform the daytime rites during the night until the end of the first watch (*prahara*), with the exception, in particular, of the *brahmayajña* and the solar rites (*saura*)."

A distinction is shown in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*: "Past rites and subsequent ones [are affected]; having indeed performed the past rites, one should then perform the subsequent ones. But he who performs the subsequent rites without having performed the past rites [does not reach] the gods, nor the ancestors, nor do humans [attain their goals]. A distinction is stated in the *Hemādri*: "In the *lājā-homa*, in the *sīmanta*, in the invocation of the deities (*devatāvāhana*), in the *arghya* offering, and in the *upasthāna*—these six have been declared by Bhṛgu."

Bharadvāja states the specific rule: "If the mantras prescribed in their respective Gṛhya-sūtras are unknown, then for those [mantras] beginning with the *upavīta* and so forth, a twice-born man should, in their recitation, use either the *praṇava* alone or the triad of *vyāhṛtis*. These two [alternatives] apply to all branches of the Vedas among the classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, another rule is stated: "But when a substitute has been taken up and the primary substance becomes available, one should not disregard the primary; rather, one should complete the rite using the secondary [substitute] alone."

When the primary [substance] is unavailable and a secondary one has been employed, but that secondary substance perishes, then a secondary substance similar to the primary should be taken, but not one similar to the secondary. However, when the primary substance is lost and one employs a substitute with the intention of substitution, if the primary object is not obtained, that very substitute must indeed be accepted. But when any secondary substance has been employed and the primary is no longer present, one who employs another substance—whether of the same class or of a different class—after taking it up, shall obtain the full result of the original rite.

Indeed, even if it is unfit for consecration (*saṃskāra*), that which is primary is accepted; however, even if it is fit for consecration, a mere imitation is not accepted. Likewise, in terms of form, color, milk, flowers, fruits, scents, and tastes, that which is similar should be taken, each subsequent one being used in the absence of the preceding. For the purpose of an oblation (*havya*), cow’s ghee (*ghṛta*) is to be taken; in its absence, buffalo ghee; or clarified butter (*ājya*); and if even that is unavailable, lac-resin oil shall be taken. This applies when no other sacrificial offerings whatsoever are available.

According to the opinion of the sage Bharadvāja, the final [alternative] in every case is to be adopted. Regarding what is stated here as the uniformity of instruction for these various causes (*nimitta*), one should understand that this applies to all such causes. Even after consuming sugarcane, water, fruit, betel, milk, or medicine, one must perform rites such as bathing and giving gifts. One may likewise employ the gift of a cow, a female slave, or a maiden while still standing. Furthermore, there are specific rules of dharma such as [performing the rite] with a child, hair, or the hand, or by pouring water into whose hand [the recipient stands]. These are the particularities of dharma.

Regarding the instruction on Dharma: the instruction on Dharma is now set forth for the purpose of practicing the Dharma previously described. On this matter, Manu says: "The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, is called Brahmāvarta, created by the gods. Kurukṣetra, Mātsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, immediately following Brahmāvarta. That which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country)."

Vinaśana is the place where the Sarasvatī disappears. "From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, the wise know the region between those two mountains to be Āryāvarta. Among the aforementioned regions, each preceding one is praised more highly than the next. Thus Sumantu says: "Brahmāvarta is the supreme region; next is the land of the Ṛṣis (Ṛṣideśa); then indeed is Madhyadeśa, and after that is Āryāvarta."

Manu further states that in the absence of these four [types of regions], another kind of region is as follows: "That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature should be known as the land of sacrifice (yajñadeśa); beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. Even when the aforementioned types are unavailable, Viṣṇu declares that a region where the social order of the four castes is observed is also a meritorious land: "That country in which the establishment of the four castes exists should be known as the land of Dharma; beyond that is Āryāvarta."

Saṃvarta, Yājñavalkya, Vasiṣṭha, and Śaṅkha declare that Āryāvarta is the region inhabited by the black antelope. Regarding these aforementioned regions, Manu states an exception: "One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by heretics, nor in one frequented by outcaste men. Even regarding this, Pitāmaha states an exception: "Even in a Śūdra country, one may dwell where the Gaṅgā flows through its midst; that is a most meritorious land, even if inhabited by non-Aryans."
Thus; here, the word "Jāhnavī" indicates not only the river itself, but also the region associated with its sacred bathing places and temples.

Prohibited Regions: Now, regarding prohibited regions, Bodhāyana states: "Ānarta, Aṅga, Magadha, Saurāṣṭra, Dakṣiṇāpatha, Upāvṛt, Sindhu, and Sauvīra—these are of mixed origin. The Āditya Purāṇa describes the fault in traveling to those regions: "Having gone to the far bank of the Narmadā, the Sindhu, or the Kauśikī, or to the western part of Padma, one incurs hell even by staying there for a time longer than that required for a pilgrimage. Likewise, Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Ugra, Mālavika, and whatever lies to the south of the Narmadā and to the north of the Sindhu [are forbidden].

"The Pauṇḍras, Caidyas, Māgadhas, and Kaṣas—one should not perform marriage, śrāddha, or sacrifice among them. Whatever sinful regions there are, inhabited by people devoted to evil deeds—by going to those impure lands, one incurs the full measure of sin. A twice-born man who goes out of desire to Saurāṣṭra, Sindhu-Sauvīra, Avantī, the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha), and the five Kaliṅgas, shall fall [from his caste]. Thus it is said.

The favor shown toward those twice-born (dvija) individuals for the sake of their livelihood during times of distress is demonstrated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "A twice-born man may always reside in Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Āndhra, Pārvatya, Kaśmīra, as well as Sindhu, Sauvīra, Saurāṣṭra, Pārada, Arāṭṭa, and Mālava; however, he should avoid them when not in distress. A householder distressed for a livelihood may take refuge in these [countries] only in extreme distress. This concludes the description of prohibited regions.

An Exception to Prohibited Regions: Now, an exception regarding certain prohibited regions is stated. Pitāmaha says: "Even in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, one may dwell where the Jāhnavī flows through its midst; that is a most meritorious region, even if inhabited by non-Aryans. In the *Dharmaśāstrasāra*: "Expiations such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, Kṛcchra, and Mahāsāntapana are prescribed for those places where the Gaṅgā is not found. The meaning of the word "Gaṅgā" is also defined in that very same work: "The Kāverī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and Gautamī..."

"The five Gaṅgās are proclaimed as being renowned as the Bhāgīrathī. Thus [it is said]. In the Āditya Purāṇa: "That region where the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, flows is indeed the most excellent forest; that should be known as a field of the Siddhas, situated upon the banks of the Gaṅgā. At Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Kāśī, Naimiṣa, Amarakuṇḍaka, on the Gaṅgā, and on the banks of the Sarayū, righteous people shall dwell," and so forth. This concludes the exception regarding prohibited regions.

Now, regarding local customs (*deśadharma*): indeed, five types of practices are observed among the people of the South (*dākṣiṇātya*). These are: eating together with a son who has not yet undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), as well as with a widow; likewise, the marriage of a daughter to her father’s sister or her maternal uncle’s son; the consumption of stale food; the sale of wool; making one’s living through arms; and maritime trade across the ocean. Furthermore, traveling by boat upon the Indus is a practice of the Northerners (*udīcya*); thus, there are five such practices.

In this way, other contradictory practices are seen due to differences in locality. For instance, the taking of a brother’s wife by one who has no [other] wife, and the giving away of a daughter within the family, are seen as highly reprehensible in some regions, yet are observed in other countries. Likewise, even the marriage of a mother is seen among the Persians. If these conflicting customs were to be considered authoritative based on locality, then Bṛhaspati says: "The laws established for specific countries, castes, and families must be maintained exactly as they are; otherwise, the subjects become agitated."

Devala also says: "In whatever regions there are Vedas, in whatever regions there are twice-born, in whatever regions there is water, and whatever clay is found there; in whatever places there is purification and whatever kind of righteous conduct exists—one should not despise those things there, for such is the dharma in that very place. In whichever country, town, village, among the three Vedas, or even in a city, whatever dharma has been ordained for a particular place, one should not deviate from that dharma. Thus it is said.

Since it might follow that local customs (*deśadharma*) are authoritative without distinction, Manu states that what is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*māna*) should be accepted: "What is practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men—one should ordain that as the law for those born in that country or family, provided it is not contradictory. The meaning is: that which is practiced by the virtuous, if it is not contradicted by such authorities as the Vedas (*śruti*), one should ordain as the duty (*dharma*) for those born in that specific country, family, or caste. "Just as that which is corrupted by the scriptures must be abandoned, so too must that which is opposed to the world."

In this regard, Mihira states: "First, the local customs of each region must be considered; whatever the established practice is in a particular land, that alone should be followed. Wise men avoid what is hated by the world; therefore, the astrologer should proceed according to the ways of the people," and so forth. Thus concludes the exposition on regional laws (*deśadharma*).

The Characteristics of the Yugas. Now, regarding the characteristics of the yugas, in the Āraṇyaka Parvan: "The Kṛta is the name of the most excellent age, wherein the eternal Dharma exists. In that supreme age, everything is already accomplished; there is nothing further to be done. There, boundaries do not fail, nor indeed do the people decay. Therefore, it is called the Kṛta-yuga, having attained its qualities through time. In the Kṛta-yuga, the fourfold order of society (cāturvarṇya) is eternal in its four quarters. This is what is known as the Kṛta-yuga, which is entirely devoid of the three [inferior] qualities."

In the Tretā Yuga, Dharma diminishes by one quarter, and Acyuta (Viṣṇu) assumes a reddish hue. Men are engaged in knowledge and devoted to the performance of ritual duties; consequently, sacrifices and various religious rites proceed. In that age, people abide by their own specific duties and remain active in their observances. Viṣṇu turns yellow, and the Veda itself becomes fourfold. Indeed, there is a decline of Truth, yet some few remain established in it. For those falling away from Truth, many diseases arise.

Desires, calamities, and likewise those caused by the gods; for some desire pleasure, while others desire wealth and perform sacrifices. Thus, having reached the Dvāpara age, living beings decline through unrighteousness. O son of Kuntī, in the Kali age, Dharma stands upon only one quarter. Vedic practices subside, as do religious duties, sacrifices, and ritual acts. Famine, diseases, lethargy, faults, anger, and the like prevail. In this way, the characteristics of the ages differ according to the distinctions between the ages.

The authoritative means for understanding this distinction should be known as the beneficial words of Manu: "Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be supreme; in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone is supreme. Parāśara states that which causes the gradations in righteousness: "In the Kṛta age, a gift is given after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā ages, it is given by calling out; in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali age, it is given through service."

Regarding this, it is stated in the Mādhavīya that the plural form in the phrase "in the Tretās" (*tretāsu*) is intended to illustrate the use of the singular for the class [of ages] such as the Kṛta and Dvāpara. Parāśara describes the gradation based on the occasion: "A gift given after approaching [the recipient] is the highest; one given by summoning [him] is middling; one given to one who begs is the lowest; but a gift given through service is fruitless."

Regarding the authority of Dharma according to the division of the Yugas, it is said: "In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu are authoritative; in the Tretā, those of Gautama are recorded; in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are recorded. He also states what constitutes a ground for unrighteousness: "In the Kṛta age, one should abandon the country; in the Tretā, one should leave the village; in the Dvāpara, the single family; but in the Kali age, the perpetrator alone. If a fallen man resides in a country consisting of a collection of villages, he brings about unrighteousness and must therefore be abandoned in the Kṛta age.

The same should be applied to villages and other such places. In the *Mādhavīya*, it is shown that "abandoning the agent" means avoiding conversation and other forms of interaction with him. Parāśara explains the various types of sins as follows: "In the Kṛta age, one falls merely by conversing; in the Tretā, by touching; in the Dvāpara, by taking food; but in the Kali age, one falls through the act itself. The meaning is that in the Kali age, one becomes an outcaste through acts such as killing, and not merely through conversation and the like.

He himself explains the duration of the results of curses from a guru and others by dividing them: "In the Kṛta age, the curse is instantaneous; in the Tretā, it lasts for ten days; in the Dvāpara, for one month; but in the Kali age, it lasts for a year. Regarding the division of time for the accomplishment of dharma, it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "That which [is accomplished] in ten years in the Kṛta age, in the Tretā it is done in a year; in the Dvāpara, that same thing is done in a month, and in the Kali age, in a single day and night."

Regarding the distinction of sacred fords according to the divisions of the Yugas, the Viṣṇudharmottara states: "Puṣkara should be resorted to in the Kṛta age, likewise Naimiṣa in the Tretā; in the Dvāpara, however, Kurukṣetra, and in the Kali age, one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā."

The characteristics of the Kali Yuga are described in detail. Regarding this, Vyāsa says: "That which one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara, one attains that in the Kali age simply by chanting the name of Keśava. Furthermore: "In the Kali age, a person attains an extraordinary excellence of dharma with very little effort; therefore, O knowers of dharma, I am pleased with the Kali age."

A specific detail is stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "That dharma which belongs to the Kṛta Yuga must not be practiced in the Kali Yuga, because in the Kali Yuga both women and men are addicted to sin. There is no learning, no pure wealth, and no purity of mind in the Kali Yuga; therefore, truth alone is beneficial for men. The term *kārtayuga* means "pertaining to that [Kṛta] Yuga. In the *Āraṇyaparvan*, the condition of the people in the Kali Yuga is described: "Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas become intermingled with one another."

"They will become equal to Śūdras, devoid of austerity and truth; by their very nature, men will be performers of cruel deeds and suspicious of one another when the dissolution of the Yuga has arrived. Thus it is said. Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Maitreya, when the Kali age has arrived, people corrupted by heresy will not worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, the creator of all. Everyone will claim to speak the Veda, O Maitreya, yet they will not practice it, being devoted only to their genitals and bellies."

Thus it is said. Parāśara also states: "In the Kali age, dharma is indeed conquered by adharma, and truth by falsehood; kings are conquered by thieves, and men by women. The *agnihotra* sacrifices fall into decay, the worship of gurus perishes, and maidens give birth [to children] while that Kali age prevails. Just as the Kali age increases, so too does the increase of unrighteousness (*adharma*). As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Whenever there is a decline of the virtuous who follow the path of the Vedas..."

"Then and there the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise: when there is no delight in the declarations of the Vedas and a fondness for heretics, then and there the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise. And so forth. Furthermore, it is said: "In the Kṛta age, the life-force resides in the bones; in the Tretā, it rests in the flesh; in the Dvāpara, in the blood; but in the Kali, it is situated in food and such. Thus, Parāśara has also described the results according to the power of the ages: "In each age there are specific duties, and in those [duties] there are specific twice-born ones..."

"One should not speak ill of them, for those twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the Yugas. Thus [it is said]. In the Āraṇyaparvan: "The earth, rivers, trees, mountains, Siddhas, and likewise the celestial rishis, as well as all states of being, conform to Time in each successive Yuga," and so forth. Such are the characteristics of the Yugas.
In the Kali age, these are prohibited.

Now, regarding the duties forbidden in the Kali Yuga—the *Āditya Purāṇa* states: "Prolonged celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), marriage with a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or the same ancestral line (*sapiṇḍa*), the slaughter of a cow, the human sacrifice (*naramedha*) and the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), and the drinking of intoxicants—these should be avoided by the twice-born in the Kali age. Furthermore, the remarriage of a married woman, the inheritance of a special share for the eldest son, the slaughter of a cow, the taking of a brother's wife, and the water-pot—these five things one should not perform in the Kali age. Thus it is said.

*Kratu* also says: "The procreation of a son by the brother-in-law is permitted; a daughter is not given away [in marriage]; no killing of a cow should be performed at a sacrifice; and in the Kali age, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is not used. Likewise, there are other authorities based on the consensus of those who know the Dharma, such as: "The appointment of a brother-in-law for the procreation of offspring upon a widow; the marriage of a girl whose virginity remains intact with another suitor (meaning a remarriage even after she has been betrothed, prior to her union with a man); and the marriage of girls of other castes by the twice-born."

The killing of foremost brahmins who are aggressors in a righteous war; the taking on board of a brahmin traveling by boat upon the ocean, even if he has been purified; the initiation for a long sacrificial session (*sattra*) for all castes; the carrying of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); setting out on the Great Journey (*mahāprasthāna*); the immolation of cows in the *gosava* sacrifice; the drinking of liquor in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice; eating the remnants from a sacrificial cup (*camasa*); licking the oblation-ladle used in the *agnihotra*; the consumption of what has been licked and the failure to accept what has been licked; and entering the forest hermitage (*vānaprastha*) stage as enjoined by rule—[all these are forbidden].

For an ascetic, begging for alms from all castes according to the prescribed rule; the offering of water for ten days for a corpse; the gift of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as directed by the preceptor; the shortening of the period of ritual impurity (aghasaṅkocana) based on one's conduct and Vedic study; the prescription of expiations (prāyaścitta) for Brahmins that end only with death; the taint of association with thieves and others; the atonement for mortal sins (mahāpātaka); the act of sacrificing animals for gods, guests, and ancestors; and the formal acceptance of sons other than the "given" (datta) or "adopted" (aurasa) types—these are forbidden.

Likewise, association with the wicked—even those who have been purified—is forbidden for those of equal caste. When a marriage is contracted with a man of lower status, one must abandon the wife of a Guru.
