Furthermore, touching the body after the collection of bones has taken place, as well as exercising ownership over Brahmins and selling Soma, are prohibited. Bringing food from one who performs base occupations, such as eating the food of Śūdras who are slaves, cowherds, family friends, or sharecroppers, is forbidden. Likewise, for a householder, visiting sacred pilgrimage sites from afar is not permitted.

This refers to matters other than pilgrimages to the Gaṅgā and similar sites, according to the statement: "In the Kali age, one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā. Likewise, the feeding of Brahmins [is permitted] during an eclipse; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, [the same applies to their respective duties]; and the conduct toward the wife of a guru is said to be that of a disciple. Furthermore, the practice of not providing for the morrow (living from hand to mouth) is the mode of subsistence for the foremost of the twice-born in times of distress. Moreover, the taking of another's wife for the sake of progeny, the wandering of Brāhmaṇas, the act of blowing upon fire with the mouth, and the acceptance of women who have been defiled by force and the like, are enjoined by sacred law.

For Śūdras, even the act of cooking for Brāhmaṇas and others; the practice of leaping into the Bhṛgu-fall or fire, as well as the death of the elderly and so forth; the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) from milk left over after satisfying cows; the imposition of punishment upon witnesses in disputes between father and son; and the taking up of household life by an ascetic—these practices were prohibited at the beginning of the Kali age by wise and high-souled beings intent on the truth, for the sake of protecting the world, according to established rules.
"And the agreement of the virtuous shall also be authoritative, like the Veda. Thus end the duties to be avoided in the Kali age.
Thus ends the section on the introduction.
Now begins the section on the determination of time (*kālanirṇaya*).

The nature of time and its specific divisions: since ritual action (*karman*) is accomplished through time, the nature of time and its specific divisions are now determined. Furthermore, the dependence of ritual action—whether prescribed by the *Śruti* or the *Smṛti*—upon time is evident from such scriptural passages as, "On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," which shows that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña depends on the time of the new moon and the afternoon; likewise: "Having bathed on the new moon day, one should offer black sesame seeds and water to the ancestors."

"One should offer food according to the prescribed rule; by that, one's progeny increases"—thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Furthermore, because the offering of water with sesame seeds and other rites is dependent on specific times, as well as [the injunctions]: "On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should not study nor cause others to study; one should not cut fresh wood, nor eat another's food"; and "On the new moon day, one should not approach even a wife whose time has arrived."

Because injunctions and prohibitions—such as "one should not touch raw oil" and "one should not cut down trees"—are dependent upon a specified time, and likewise because [injunctions] such as "one should sacrifice on every full moon day" and "one offers the evening oblation and the morning oblation on every new moon day" are understood to be dependent upon time, it should be understood that time is indeed a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, not its primary constituent (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, that time is of two kinds: general (*sāmānyarūpa*) and specific (*viśeṣarūpa*).

Pervading all specific durations of time and inferable from the positions of the stars, planets, and so forth, is *sāmānyakāla* (general time); *nimeṣa* and other such units are its specific divisions. As it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "A vessel made of copper weighing six *karṣas*, thirty *aṅgulas* in width and four *aṅgulas* in height; having fashioned it with a single *mātrā* of gold and pierced at its center with tubes each weighing one *karṣa* of four *aṅgulas*, it is known as a *ghaṭikā*."

The time required for a vessel to be filled with water flowing from its rim is called a *nāḍikā*; a sixtieth part of that is a *vināḍikā*. Two *nāḍikās* constitute a *muhūrta*, fifteen of those make a day; likewise, night, fortnight, month, season, solstice, and year are formed in this manner. Thus it is said.

Names of the Years: These years are sixty in number, distinguished by the cycle beginning with *prabhava*. As it has been said: *Prabhava*, *vibhava*, *śukla*, *pramoda*, and then *prajāpati*; *āṅgīrasa*, *śrīmukha*, *bhāva*, and then the year *yuvan*; *dhātṛ*, *īśvara*, *bahudhānya*, *pramāthī*, *vikrama*, *viṣu*; *citrabhānu*, *svabhānu*, *tāraṇa*, *pārthiva*, and *vyaya*; *sarvajit*, *sarvadhārī*, *virodhī*, *vikṛti*, and *khara*.

Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, Durmukhī, Hemalambī, Vilambī, Vikārī, Śārvarī, Plava, Śubhakṛt, Krodhī, Viśvāvasu, Parābhava, Plavaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, Virodhikṛt, Parīdhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, Nala, Piṅgala, Kālayuktākṣī, Siddhārthī, Raudrī, Durmatī, Dundubhī, Rudhurodgārī, Raktākṣī, Krodhana, and Kṣaya. Thus [ends the list].

The determination of the lunar and other years: regarding that, it is stated in the *Dīpikā* that the commencement of the lunar years, such as Prabhava and the rest, is on the first day (pratipad) of the month of Caitra—"the lunar [year] begins with the first day of the bright fortnight of Madhu (Caitra). The commencement of the solar years, such as Prabhava and the rest, occurs when the sun is situated in Aries (*meṣa*). The civil (*sāvana*) year, however, is optional. As for what is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "When the moon and the sun are in the constellation of Indra (Pūrvaphalgunī) at the beginning of the bright fortnight of Māgha, and Jupiter and Venus are likewise positioned, that is traditionally known as the start of the sixty-year cycle."

Thus, it has been stated that the years begin with the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha. This is for the purpose of explaining the auspicious and inauspicious results well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), and not for the purpose of the performance of ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*); this should be understood, because only that which begins at the start of the year is useful for such performance. To this effect, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa says: "One should always remember the lunar year (*cāndra-saṃvatsara*) everywhere at the commencement of rituals; one should not [remember] another, because its commencement is proclaimed to be at the beginning of the year."

In this regard, the intermediate subdivisions of the lunar year are stated: "The first is the *saṃvatsara*, the second is the *parivatsara*, the third is the *iḍāvatsara*, and the fourth is the *anuvatsara*. The fifth is the *udvatsara*; the collection of these is known as a *yuga*. Thus, from *prabhava* up to *kṣaya*, there are twelve sets of five years. Within each such set of five, the *saṃvatsara* and the others occur in sequence. All of this is well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).

It is not written here for fear of prolixity. The application of the three [types of months], namely the solar and the others, has been shown by Jyotir-Garga: "The solar month is prescribed for marriage and the like; the *sāvana* [lunar] month is remembered for sacrifices and the like; and the lunar month is praised for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies (*pitṛkārya*). Here, by the first "and the like" (*ādi*), initiation (*upanayana*), worship, vows, observances, consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), house-building, journeys, and so forth are included. By the second "and the like," there is the inclusion of giving gifts, fire-offerings (*homa*), impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), birth-rites (*jātakarma*), debts, purchases, and business transactions. "Annual" refers to the *śrāddha* performed on the anniversary of the day of death. "Ancestral ceremony" (*pitṛkārya*)...

And in cases such as the six-monthly *śrāddha* and others—by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is stated in the *Hemādri* that the lunar month (*cāndra-māsa*) is recommended for every single undertaking, with the exception of those sacrifices (*yajña*) accomplished over a month or a year.

Now, an objection may be raised: since rites such as marriage are undertaken according to the *sāvana* (lunar) month—as seen in injunctions like "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years"—how can it be said that "the solar month is for marriage and so forth"? Likewise, since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is prescribed for the new moon of Vaiśākha in the text "He who establishes the fires on the new moon of Vaiśākha," and since the solar month is also prescribed for marriage, vows, and sacrifices by the statement "The solar measure is praised for marriage, vows, and sacrifices," how can it be that the *sāvana* is used for sacrifices and the like? Furthermore, [it is forbidden] when the sun is in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus, or during the dark fortnights...

If it is asked: "Since the performance of ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) is prescribed even by the solar measure (*sauramāna*) in such passages as 'By this method one should here perform the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors,' how can it be said that 'for the annual ancestral rite, the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*) is recommended'? The answer is: No. These measures, such as the solar and others, are applicable in certain specific rituals, while in others they are optional alternatives. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the *tilaka-vrata* should be performed. And that must be performed according to the lunar measure alone.

This is because the first days of the bright and dark fortnights depend upon the solar and civil (sāvana) reckonings. As for what is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*—"When the sun has entered Aries, O best of men, one should observe a fast"—referring to vows such as the *Sujanmāvāpti*, that must be performed according to the solar reckoning alone. However, rites such as the *Gavām ayana*, which are accomplished over the course of a year, must be performed according to the civil (sāvana) reckoning alone; for the lunar month is deficient by six days and nights, whereas the solar month is exceeded by five days and nights.

Even in the case of the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice, it must be performed according to the lunar month (*cāndra*), because the authors of the Sūtras prescribe its performance on lunar lunar days (*tithi*) in the rule: "on the new moon day and on the full moon day. Thus, in such instances, the year that presents itself is the lunar one. However, in other cases, such as initiation (*upanayana*) and marriage (*vivāha*), there is an option (*vikalpa*), as stated in the *Mādhavīya*. Others, however, say that based on the natural force of the word "is praised" (*praśasyate*), a particular [calendar] is recommended for certain [rites]. In this way, the application of the lunar and other types of years should be understood.
This is the determination of the year.

The utility of determining the year: The utility of this determination of the year is stated as follows—“O Blessed One! By what action is a person not born into the womb of an animal, nor in a barbarian land? Tell me that, O Sage! Mārkaṇḍeya said: “When the sun enters Aries, the best of the twice-born, having observed a fast...”

Beginning with "One should worship the divine Bhārgava Rāma according to one's ability and according to the rules," and ending with "At the transit of the sun into Pisces (Mīna), one should worship the Fish [incarnation] and Vāsudeva," there is the *Sujanmavrata* as described by Mārkaṇḍeya. Furthermore, regarding monthly and annual rites, as well as on occasions of prosperity such as the acquisition of clothing, grain, gold, and so forth, and for the provision of servants and the like, the solar and civil (sāvana) months and years are to be used.

Such activities as these, as well as the Ananta-vrata and other observances mentioned in passages such as "the vow of Ananta is to be performed for nine and five years," and likewise the Aśūnya-śayana-vrata and others described in the Bhāgavata, as well as all rites to be completed within a year—all these constitute its fruit.

The Determination of the Yugas. Now follows the determination of the yugas. Manu describes the nature of the yugas according to the sequence of days and nights of the ancestors (pitṛs) and the gods (devas), and so forth: "In the reckoning of the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night, with the division [of time] occurring by means of the two fortnights. For the performance of ritual acts, the dark fortnight is the day, while the bright fortnight is the night for sleep. The phrase 'the division is stated' is to be understood as the ellipsis. 'For the performance of ritual acts' means for the purpose of performing ritual acts. "In the reckoning of the gods, a year constitutes a day and a night; their division is as follows: the northern course of the sun (udagayana) is the day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is the night."

Now learn in brief the measure of a single day and night of Brahmā, and the duration of each of the Yugas in their proper order. "Of Brahmā" means of Hiraṇyagarbha. The Kṛta Yuga is said to consist of four thousand years; its dawn (sandhyā) consists of as many hundreds, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is of the same duration. "Years" refers to divine years. Dawn is the time at the commencement of a Yuga; twilight is the time at the conclusion of a Yuga.

In the other three ages—the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—along with their respective junctions (saṃdhyās) and sub-junctions (saṃdhyāṃśas), the thousands and hundreds decrease by one. "By one" means by the omission of one. This four-age cycle (caturyuga) which has been enumerated at the outset consists of twelve thousand [years]; this is called a yuga of the gods. A thousand-fold enumeration of these divine yugas should be known as a single day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration. Thus it is said.

Also in the Āraṇyaparvan of the Mahābhārata: "They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years; its dawn (sandhyā) is as many hundreds, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is the same thereafter. Tretā, by measure, consists of three thousand years; its dawn is as many hundreds, and its twilight is the same thereafter. Then, Dvāpara consists of two thousand years by measure; its dawn is two hundred, and its twilight is the same thereafter."

The Kali Yuga is recorded as lasting one thousand years; its dawn (saṃdhyā) and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) each consist of one hundred years. Understand that the measure of the dawn and the twilight is equal. When the Kali Yuga has exhausted, the Kṛta Yuga begins. This number of twelve thousand [years] is proclaimed as the duration of a Yuga-cycle. A period of one thousand such cycles is declared to be a single day of Brahmā. And so forth. Thus ends the determination of the Yugas.

The determination of the seasons (*ṛtu-nirṇaya*). Now follows the determination of the solstices (*ayana*) in their proper order. Because the sun travels toward the southern direction by means of these three seasons, a triad of seasons constitutes an *ayana*. Thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, the Āditya goes southward for six months, and he goes northward for six months. This, however, refers specifically to the solar [measure], because it proceeds depending upon the sun.

Regarding this, what should be performed during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) and what is prohibited during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is set forth in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "Entering a house, the installation of deities, marriage, the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the investiture of the sacred thread (*mauñjī*), and the binding of vows—rites such as these yield auspicious results during the northern course; however, those that are forbidden should indeed be performed during the southern course. It is stated in the *Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā* that the installation of fierce deities (*ugradevatā*) and similar rites should be performed during the southern course: "The Mothers, Bhairava, Varāha, Narasiṃha, and Trivikrama..."
"The destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura should indeed be installed during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana). Thus ends the determination of the solstices.

Now follows the determination of the seasons (*ṛtunirṇaya*). The word *ṛtu* is derived from the verbal root *ṛ*, meaning "to go" or "to move. Thus, the word *ṛtu* denotes specific periods of time such as spring and so forth, as they "move on" or "pass away. According to the *Mādhavīya*, this season is to be inferred by its unique characteristics, such as the blooming of the *aśoka* flowers. Some maintain that this word *ṛtu* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a pair of months that constitutes a division of the year. That season is sixfold: spring (*vasanta*), summer (*grīṣma*), the rains (*varṣā*), autumn (*śarat*), winter (*hemanta*), and the cool season (*śiśira*). Regarding this, the Vedic scripture states: "There are indeed six seasons."

If it is objected: "How can there be six seasons when the Vedic scripture states, 'There are twelve months and five seasons'?"—it is not so; for the number five is established by the intention of treating Hemanta and Śiśira as one, as evidenced by the scriptural text: "I gratify the two seasons, Hemanta and Śiśira, among the seasons. These seasons, beginning with Vasanta, are of two kinds: lunar (*cāndra*) and solar (*saura*). They are called lunar because they are determined by the motion of the moon.

Regarding the seasons beginning with spring (*vasanta*), Bodhāyana states: "Spring is either the [period of] Pisces and Aries, or Aries and Taurus. Thus, he accepts that the commencement of spring may optionally begin with Pisces or with Aries. Accordingly, the summer (*grīṣma*) and subsequent seasons are also optionally determined as appropriate. Their application is to be understood from such injunctions as: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring," and "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring."

Regarding this, the author of the *Trikāṇḍī* states the superiority of the lunar [months]: "One should perform all rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis during the lunar seasons; in their absence, however, during the solar seasons—such is the opinion of the astronomers. Thus ends the determination of the seasons.

The Determination of the Month: Now, the determination of the month is being made. That specific period of time in which the moon's increase, wane, and so forth are measured (masyate) is a *māsa*. It is of three kinds, distinguished as lunar (*cāndra*), solar (*sāvana*), and sidereal (*saura*). As it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "The lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon; the solar month is the duration of time during which the sun remains in a single zodiacal sign, consisting of thirty solar days."

The lunar month (*cāndro māsaḥ*) is of two kinds: that which begins with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) and ends with the new moon (*darśa*), and that which begins with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*) and ends with the full moon (*pūrṇimā*). Among these, the former is established by Śruti and Smṛti, such as: "Having completed the months with the new moon, they leave off the day," and "Where Indra and Agni are offered, that is proclaimed as the beginning of the month; likewise, when Agni and Soma are in the middle, and the Pitṛs and Soma at the end. It is also stated: "The lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon. The second kind, however, is described as: "Having completed the months with the full moon, they leave off the day."

This is established by such scriptural passages as, "For on the full moon day one perceives the months," and so forth. Here, it is understood that between the two [alternatives], the scripture has a greater inclination toward the month ending with the full moon.

By means of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) beginning with "He who indeed draws from the full [jar]" and ending with "they descend toward the sacrifice," and by the statement in the *Ātharvaṇa*—"Prajāpati is indeed the month; his dark fortnight is wealth (rayi), and his bright fortnight is the vital breath (prāṇa)"—which identifies the dark fortnight as primary; likewise, [it is said]: "The Śrāddha should be performed day after day during the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja; [specifically] on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada at midnight."

It is understood from such Smṛti texts as, "In the month of Proṣṭhapada, that [tithi] is remembered by the name Jayantī," and so forth; furthermore, it is inferred because the injunction for Jayantī on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada would otherwise be untenable given the rule for the Mahālaya in the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja. For instance, if the month were reckoned by the new moon (darśānta), it would be impossible for the Mahālaya dark fortnight to fall within Āśvayuja while Jayantī falls within Bhādrapada; thus, this inconsistency leads one to understand that the month is reckoned by the full moon (paurṇamāsyanta).

Likewise, in the section concerning ascetics (*yati*), it is well known that shaving at the junctions of the seasons is prescribed for them by such Smṛti texts as "one should shave at the junctions of the seasons. This is also established by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). Now, if the month did not end with the full moon (*paurṇimānta*), then because the new moon (*darśa*) alone would constitute the seasonal junction, the shaving would necessarily occur only then and not on the full moon day; yet it does occur then. Therefore, it is understood through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*) that [the month must indeed end with the full moon].

Likewise, because the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas) is observed regarding the month ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī) in rites such as the Māghasnāna; and similarly, in certain cases such as the Cāturmāsya vows, it is prescribed that the vegetable fast (śākavrata) and other observances should be performed starting from the tenth day of the bright fortnight until the tenth day of the bright fortnight—therefore, that [lunar] month should also be understood as one [to be reckoned]. The scriptural authorities for this will be clarified later. Consequently, the month ending with the full moon is the more prevalent.

Likewise, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* demonstrates the lunar mansion month (*nākṣatra-māsa*): "The lunar mansion month is said to consist of the complete revolution of all the asterisms. The solar [month] is determined by the first and last signs of the zodiac. The civil month (*sāvana*) is said to be a calculation of thirty days; in that case, human intention and the like are the determining factors. In the lunar mansion [month], the asterism is the determining factor—this rule should be observed everywhere."

The application of the lunar months ending with the new moon (darśānta) and others has been shown in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "For a Brāhmaṇa, the month should be delimited by the new moon; likewise for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, [it is delimited] by the solar ingress (saṅkrānti) and the full moon (paurṇamāsī). Similarly, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, in the section on the greatness of the month (mādyamāhātmya), a specific distinction is stated: "That month which begins on the tenth day and ends on the tenth day is for auspicious rites; for ritualists it begins with the full moon, and for the ancestors it begins with the solar ingress. One should undertake the vow (vrata) starting from whichever of these alternatives is appropriate, and so forth.

Thus, for the two kinds of twelve lunar months, the designations beginning with Caitra are determined by their connection to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). The month in which the full moon is conjoined with a lunar mansion such as Citrā is Caitra and so forth. Even when there is no direct conjunction with that [specific] mansion, a pair of lunar mansions serves as the determinant for the five months beginning with Caitra. The division should be understood as follows: for the sixth and seventh [months], there is a triad of three; for the four months from the eighth to the eleventh, there is a pair of two for each; and for the last [month], there is a triad of three.

This has been stated in the *Saṅkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*: "When the pairs of stars beginning with Citrā are in conjunction with the full moon, the months beginning with Caitra are to be known; [these] are determined by groups of three, starting from the sixth, the last, and the seventh. Elsewhere also: "The last two and the penultimate [months] are to be known as having three [stars]; Phālguna is considered to have three [stars]; the remaining months are to be known as having two [stars], according to the arrangement beginning with Kṛttikā. Also in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakabhāṣya*: "When the pair of stars beginning with Citrā is joined with the full moon, the months beginning with Caitra are to be understood," and so forth.

In this context, the general term "month" is employed in the *Taittirīyaka* and other texts, as in: "It is performed for the ancestors every month," and "Every month they perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants; every month the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn. In another recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is established in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice: "He offers the *agnihotra* for a month. This should be understood as proven.

Regarding the specific application for particular months, the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Māhātmya* of Vaiśākha, states: "Just as ghee is superior to curd, so too is the month of Ūrja (Kārttika) superior; the month of Māgha is superior to Kārttika, and Vaiśākha is indeed superior to Māgha. Religious merit performed in that [Vaiśākha] month increases like the seed of a banyan tree. Likewise, in the *Māgha-māhātmya* of the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "If one is unable to perform the morning bath, the wise person should perform it for three months: when the sun is situated in Libra (Tulā) and when the sun is in Capricorn (Makara)."

"One should always perform the morning bath with diligence during the month of Meṣa (Aries); that lowest of men who does not perform the morning bath during these three months goes to the Raurava hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Kārttika-māsa-māhātmya*: "In whichever house the festival of the month of Māgha for Viṣṇu is observed, one is not tainted by the sins arising from the Kali age, even those already committed. And likewise in that same work: "They know Kārttika to yield a thousandfold fruit compared to all other months."

Therefore, Janārdana declared that Māgha possesses a hundred thousandfold merit. There is no dharma superior to the Māgha bath; there is no higher goal than the Māgha bath. There is no gain greater than the Māgha bath; there is no supreme refuge other than the Māgha bath. That lowest of men who does not perform the morning bath in the month of Māgha enters a Piśāca womb and remains there until the dissolution of all beings. Likewise, in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "And he who bathes in Vaiśākha when the sun is situated in Aries..."

"On the Kāverī river, or during the month of Tulā, Kārttika, or even Māgha. Likewise, in that same work: "On the full moon day of Kārttika, Vaiśākha, or Caitra, for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors, the householder who does not offer an umbrella and divine refreshment (pānaka). Furthermore: "In the month of Kārmuka (Mārgaśīrṣa), he who does not offer mung-bean rice to Viṣṇu; nor curd-rice in Vaiśākha; nor refreshment on the new moon day of Caitra; nor curd-rice in Vaiśākha for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors."

"One who does not worship Mādhava at dawn during the Cāturmāsya, one who does not perform the lamp-worship of Viṣṇu in the month of Kārttika, and one who does not give an umbrella to a Brahmin in Kārttika"—in such passages, the application [of the term] should be seen in reference to monthly rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts. In the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, in the speech of Bharata, the fault is to be seen as follows: "O Mother, whatever sin these have committed, may that be mine, if I am a defiler of Rāma."

A specific feature of Dhanurmāsa is described in that very same work, in the fifty-second chapter concerning Dhanurmāsa: "In Dhanurmāsa, Hari is certainly pleased by worship performed at the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla). He bestows the desired fruit inexhaustibly; I tell you this as the truth. Having bathed at dawn during Dhanurmāsa and having properly worshipped Janārdana, one should offer food made of mung beans with curd. Furthermore, one should feed the best of the twice-born at the morning hour according to one's capacity."

"Having enjoyed all pleasures here, you shall indeed attain the station of Viṣṇu. During the month of Dhanus, at dawn, having offered to Hari the delightful dish of curd with fresh ginger, combined with ghee, cardamom, sugar, along with *āmalaka* and radish, the wise man should feed the Brāhmaṇas. Whatever desire he may long for—even that which is very difficult to attain—he shall obtain it; he shall become a yogi, wise, and illustrious, a Vaiṣṇava in birth after birth. Thus [it is said].

The sin incurred by failing to perform [the rite] is stated in that very same place: "He who does not perform the Vaiṣṇava worship at dawn during the month of Dhanus shall remain destitute for seven births and be a fool afflicted with consumption. The further fruit resulting from its performance is stated in that very same place: "When the sun is situated in Sagittarius (Dhanus), he who offers an oblation of mung beans achieves the merit of a thousand-year worship in a single day. Just as the Lord of Ramā is pleased by the offering of mung beans in the month of Dhanus..."

Neither by vows, gifts, and charities, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, does one attain that which he attains who, having swiftly conquered his enemies, properly offers mung-bean rice with ginger to Hari when the sun is situated in Sagittarius (Kodaṇḍa). He who offers rice with curd, ginger, and mung beans to Viṣṇu during the month of Dhanus shall be long-lived, wealthy, and a master of the Vedas. For him who offers rice with ginger and mung beans to Acyuta, what need is there for bathing in the Gaṅgā, for recitations, or for sacrifices in this world?

"If one desires longevity, health, and sovereignty, [one should worship] right now indeed. Likewise, in another place: "In the month of Dhanus (Sagittarius), she should gratify the lotus-eyed Lord with food made of mung beans (*mudga*). Having offered mung-bean rice along with ginger to the Consort of Indra (Lakṣmī) for Viṣṇu, that virtuous woman, though once distressed, attained eternal sovereignty. Reciting this twelve times and worshipping Lakṣmī, and having offered jaggery and mung-bean rice in the month of Dhanus for the sake of attaining wealth, she would immediately obtain inexhaustible riches through the side-glance of Lakṣmī."

The first name of the Goddess is Śrī; the second is Amṛtodbhavā; the third is said to be Kamalā; the fourth is Lokasundarī; the fifth is Viṣṇupatnī; the sixth is Śrīvaiṣṇavī; the seventh is Varārohā; the eighth is Harivallabhā; the ninth is said to be Śārṅgiṇī; the tenth is Devadevikā; the eleventh is Mahālakṣmī; and the twelfth is Lokasundarī.

Śrī, Padmā, Kamalā, Mukundamahiṣī, Lakṣmī, Trilokeśvarī, Kṣīrābdhisutā, Aravindajanani, Vidyā, Sarojātmikā, and Sarvābhīṣṭaphalapradā—those who, being exceedingly pure, constantly recite these twelve names every morning, obtain all auspicious things. This meritorious hymn to Bhadralakṣmī always brings good fortune; having bathed in the Kāverī at Tauli, one should chant it in the presence of the Śrīvṛkṣa (Tulasi tree). Thus spoke Nārada to Yudhiṣṭhira.

In that very same work, elsewhere it says: "He who offers to Viṣṇu curd, ginger, and rice with mung beans, radiant with curd, ghee, cardamom, and jaggery—very pleasantly warm and with potatoes—the Lord of the World, who is affectionate toward His devotees, becomes pleased upon seeing that auspicious offering of rice with mung beans and bestows all enjoyments as well as liberation. There is much more of this kind elaborated here and there; it is not written down here for fear of excessive length.

Regarding the *mahāvyatīpāta* occurring during the month of Dhanus (Sagittarius), the *Āgneya Purāṇa* states: "The man who, full of devotion, bathes at dawn during the *aparkṣa* [lunar mansion] when the sun is in Sagittarius (*kārmuka*), and offers me food made of mung beans (*mudga*), is indeed the most excellent of the *bhāgavatas*. To him who gives food made of mung beans to Brahmins when the sun is in Sagittarius, I grant liberation; how much more so, then, the abundance of worldly enjoyments? Thousands of *agniṣṭoma* sacrifices and hundreds of *vājapeya* sacrifices do not equal the merit of offering mung-bean food during the *vyatīpāta* yoga when the sun is in Sagittarius."

One who has fallen from the Vedas, one who has fallen from his vows, or even an enemy, becomes purified by giving mung-bean food (*mudgānna*) to a Brahmin during the *cāpa* and *pāta* [yogas]. All the gods, sages, and ancestors, along with all the worlds and their lords, praise mung-bean food offered during the *vyatīpāta* yoga in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. Listen to the meritorious fruit for one who, having offered mung-bean food to Viṣṇu at dawn during the *cāpa*, feeds the ancestors during the *pāta*: it is as if ten thousand *śrāddhas* have been perfectly performed at the field of Gayā and the Setu of Rāma.

All the ancestors of that lineage also go to the abode of Hari. He who offers mung beans mixed with sugar, ghee, and fruits to Brahmins at dawn during the month of Dhanus—what need has he of millions of vows or of sacred fords that cause physical hardship? Those who, having bathed in the morning, worship Hari outside in the waters of the Cāpa [river], are honored by Indra and the other gods, and all beings stand in awe of them. Such a person is as if bathed in all sacred fords and in rivers such as the Kāverī.

Thousands of Ardhodayas and sacrifices such as the Vājapeya do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the Vyatīpāta yoga occurring in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. During the Vyatīpāta of Mārgaśīrṣa, a person seeking to gratify the ancestors should offer libations and present the *arghya* while meditating upon Hari with the root mantra. The root mantra is: O Vyatīpāta! O Great Being! O Destroyer of all sins! O Thousand-armed One! O Soul of the Universe! Accept this *arghya*; salutations unto You! O Vyatīpāta! Salutations unto You; salutations unto You, the Auspiciousness of the Universe!

"Salutations to You, whose divine splendor is the very form of Viṣṇu’s discus! Having thus offered one *arghya* as the prescribed measure while facing south, and having meditated upon the ancestors of both lineages, one should offer libations for the satisfaction of the Pitṛs: 'O Beloved of Viṣṇu! O Vyatīpāta! O Giver of freedom from debt to the Pitṛs! O Blessed Lord Hari, grant Vaikuṇṭha to my ancestors! By Your grace, may there be in me unwavering devotion; O Blessed Lord, grant me knowledge, realization, and dispassion.'"
Since this rite is to be accomplished during the month of Sauradhanus, it is described here.

Furthermore, regarding that subject, a specific detail is stated in that very same work, in the dialogue between Viṣṇu and Śacī: "Therefore, in the month called Dhanus (Sagittarius), having abandoned other rites at the dawn of Aruṇodaya, you who perform the worship with mung-bean food—be the bestower of liberation upon him! Worship performed at midday in the month of Dhanus becomes fruitless. Worship at the primary Aruṇodaya is the best; that when the stars have vanished [but before sunrise] is middling; that which is accompanied by the sun [after sunrise] is inferior. At midday it is fruitless. The measure of mung-beans and rice is said to be the most excellent of the excellent."

Half a *tandula* (rice grain) is the medium measure, and half of that is the lowest; some lords among sages praise double the amount of *mudga* (mung beans). One should perform the rite according to one's capacity, but not less than half a *tandula*. He who, out of the foolishness of poverty, does not offer *mudga*-food to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārmuka (Cāpa), shall remain destitute for seven births. He who, fearing a loss of merit, does not worship the Lord at dawn when the sun is in Cāpa, shall be destitute, afflicted by disease, and—being a hater of Viṣṇu—fall downward.

Just as one might consume good food by restricting it on the day of the *alpa-dvādaśī*, so too, having abandoned [worldly] activity in the morning during the month of Dhanus, one should worship Me. Also, in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* composed by Bhāskara: "The southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is night, while the northern (*uttarāyaṇa*) is day; that constitutes a divine day and night (*ahorātra*), which the wise know to be the month of Dhanus. Therefore, with every effort, day after day in the month of Dhanus, when the time of dawn has arrived, one should worship Janārdana.

"One should offer green gram rice along with the sixteen types of ritual offerings. Thus it is said. Also in the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "When the Sun has entered Sagittarius (Cāpa), one should perform a bath at dawn and worship the Lord of the World until before sunrise. Then, at the time of daybreak, the twice-born man, having offered the *arghya* water, should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra and then pay homage to the Sun. Also in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "Having worshipped Hari during the final watch of the month of Dhanus..."

"Subsequently, one should perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*); there is no loss of dharma. And in the *Pañcarātra*: "When the sun is situated in Sagittarius (*cāpa*), by worshipping Hari at dawn, the fruit of a thousand years of worship is obtained in a single day. And in the *Pārameṣṭhya*: "When the sun has entered Sagittarius, one should worship Hari at dawn according to the ritual of the Great Consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) and through the recitation of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*), etc. And in the *Yāmala*: "Especially during the time of dawn on a Sunday coinciding with the *vyatīpāta* yoga in the month of Dhanus..."

Having worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion using offerings of mung-bean rice mixed with *coṭikā*, especially with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), various kinds of foods both solid and soft, accompanied by curd-rice, as well as incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*); one should especially feed Brāhmaṇas there during the morning hours. With the remnants of Viṣṇu’s food offering, and especially with the milk-rice, one should diligently perform the gift of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth. Through such giving, O twice-born, the donor attains all desires and noble generosity. Thus it is said.

And in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, in the section on gifts (*dānakhaṇḍa*): "O best of men! By worshipping Hari at dawn during the month of Dhanus, by feeding Brāhmaṇas, and by various gifts, one eternally attains the world of Viṣṇu along with one's ancestors. And in the *Saṅgraha*: "When the sun has entered the month of Dhanus, the twice-born who rises in the morning and performs the worship of Hari attains the abode of Hari. Likewise: "In the month of Dhanus, for the pleasure of Hari, [one should offer] rice mixed with mung beans and jaggery."

"He who, having risen in the morning, offers [this], attains the station of Viṣṇu"—thus should one regard such statements concerning the specific times and materials for the means of worship during that month.

The duties of the Cāturmāsya: following the discussion of the months, the nature of the Cāturmāsya and the duties to be performed therein are now described. Its praise is found in the Varāha Purāṇa, in the *Cāturmāsyamāhātmya*, within the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha. Varāha says: "O beloved, there is a time dear to me known as Cāturmāsya; bathing, vows, recitation, and fire-offerings performed during that period are remembered as having infinite merit. Whatever act is performed to please me during other months, the merit thereof is ten-million-fold when Māgha occurs and the sun is in Capricorn."

"Even more than that, ten million-fold merit is obtained in the month of Vaiśākha; and even more than that, infinite-fold merit is obtained during the Cāturmāsya—of this there is no doubt. And its nature is described in that very same place: "The six months beginning with Āṣāḍha are declared to be the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana); the six months beginning with Pauṣa, O Goddess, are declared to be the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa). The lunar month is said to be of two kinds: ending with the new moon (darśānta) and ending with the full moon (paurṇimāntaka). Among these, the wise take the one ending with the full moon for the commencement of vows and other rites."

"Beginning from the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha until the full moon of Kārtika—this is the period for the Cāturmāsya vow and other rites," and so forth. Furthermore, its status as the best of all times is stated in that very same [text] by means of a narrative: Varāha said: "In ancient times, surrounded by all the hosts of gods upon the summit of Mount Meru, and having reached the southern solstice (yāmyāyana), all the gods then spoke: 'O Blessed One! By Your command, night has indeed arrived for us; we shall now depart to our respective abodes,' they said as they stood before me."

A dark-complexioned woman, wearing white garments and holding an axe, prostrated herself before him with all eight limbs and said: "O Lord, I am Rātri, and I entreat you. Indeed, during the southern course of the sun (Ayana), no auspicious rite such as marriage or the sacred thread ceremony is performed; therefore, I have been censured by people. O Master, my life is in vain, for I am despised by everyone. If you show me favor, then I shall live, and not otherwise. I shall indeed perform penance here for the sake of your grace."

Having spoken thus, the gods bowed again and then made this request: "O Lord! O Lord! O Ocean of Compassion! O You who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge! Show mercy so that one may attain fulfillment by traveling there during the night. Then, with a gracious heart, I granted her this most excellent boon: "Those three watches (yāmas) are dear to me; among them, the first two are very dear. Whatever action—be it recitation, charity, vows, or the like—is performed there, it shall possess infinite merit, even compared to that which is performed for eight months."

"The first month shall be Śrāvaṇa, then Nabhasya as the second; Āśvina shall be the third, and Kārtika is remembered as the fourth. During Cāturmāsya, there shall be an increase in merit day by day; no increase of merit equal to that of Kārtika has been declared by the wise. Having heard these words of mine, all the gods were then satisfied, and Rātridevī, being well-pleased, bowed down again and again. From that time forward, Cāturmāsya has been dear to me in this world.

"Whatever one performs there—such as the vow of giving and so forth—I bestow its fruit day by day with infinite merit. Therefore, for my pleasure, men who fear worldly existence should especially perform bathing, giving, and other rites there with devotion. And so on.

Now, regarding the rites to be performed there, as stated in the *Vrata-kāṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "One should begin on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and conclude on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika. Indeed, O best of Brahmins, one should conclude all other vows whose nature is fasting on the *Prabodhinī* (the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika). One should perform their fire-oblation (*homa*) and the worship of Brahmins on the twelfth day; all others, however, one should conclude on the full moon day. Thus it is said.

Now, regarding the Cāturmāsya vow, it is stated in that very same [text]: "When Acyuta has gone to sleep, what should be done by the twice-born of purified souls, or by women, during this month? What vow is to be observed? What is this rule? What is the conduct? Tell me, O best of speakers! Brahmā said: "When the sun has entered Cancer in the month of Āṣāḍha, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, the night of the gods is desired. Within that [period], Mahāviṣṇu is known by the name Upendra."

Assuming three states through various forms, the imperishable Janārdana—who is to be praised by all the gods—entered into yogic sleep. While he, the deity of the stainless ones, remains lying upon that [bed], no rites such as marriage should take place; a wise man should abandon the tonsure ceremony, the initiation, the wedding, and so forth. If they perform these out of ignorance, their death will surely follow; for how can there be happiness for those who are deprived of the auspicious gaze of the deities?

I shall describe the auspicious Cāturmāsya rite as proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti. On the ninth day, one should discard all old vessels—excluding those for liquids—and likewise clean the winnowing baskets and other utensils. Having performed purification by smearing with cow-dung and other substances, the wise man should cover the interior of the house with cloths, blankets, mats, and straw, and perform a bath with his clothes on. Then, having risen early on the tenth auspicious day, he should proceed.

Having bathed, completed his ritual duties, and returned home with his senses subdued, he should perform the anointing of the Lord and decorate the pavilion. Having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and thoroughly purified his body, he should worship Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rules. He should then duly perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the vows that are about to be described—namely, those performed on specific occasions, those for the fulfillment of desires, and likewise those that are obligatory—for all these vows pertain to those belonging to the four stages of life (āśramas).

In the first month, one should always observe the auspicious *śāka-vrata* (vegetable vow); in the second month, the unsurpassed *dadhi-vrata* (curd vow) should be observed; and in the third, the *payo-vrata* (milk vow). Now listen regarding the fourth: one desiring purity should avoid legumes and seeds that sprout from multiple parts. O best of Brahmins, the wise declare these vows to be obligatory. A wise man should renounce the citron, the black gram, the *tuvara*, the royal mung bean, and all unwholesome vegetables during the four months of the rainy season.

On the twelfth and the tenth days, one should renounce ten kinds of vegetables. Ten types of vegetables are declared to be avoided during the auspicious *śākavrata*: leaves, flowers, fruits, stalks, roots, buds, sesame flour, sprouts, mushrooms, and meat. These are the ten kinds of vegetables prescribed as forbidden by those established in the performance of vows. On the full moon day of Kārttika, a wise man should avoid legumes and multi-seeded grains; that which has grown from a seed is considered a "dvidala" (split-seed) unless it is a mere sprout.

That which is seen among grains as having two parts is called "two-parted" (dvidala) by the wise; likewise, that which is seen to split when struck with a stone is to be known as two-parted—listen to me as I describe it. These include the mung bean (māṣa), the green gram (mudga), the chickpea (caṇaka), the lentil (masūraka), the horse-gram (kulattha), the flat bean (niṣpāva), the āḍhaka, the kidney bean (rājamāṣaka), the black gram (rājamudga), the tamarind (tintriṇī), and the five types of nails (nakhapañcaka). One should avoid all of these, whether they be fresh or old.

O Nārada, many seeds are indeed seen within the stalk and the fruit; therefore, they say that it is "many-seeded" (bahubīja), as is the case with the *patrakīra* and other such fruits. One should perform the morning bath and the offering of lamps especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, and one whose senses are restrained should observe a vigil on the Prabodhinī day. Having given a pair of cows to his preceptor on the twelfth lunar day, he should feed the twice-born. The wise man should spend the remainder of the day until mid-afternoon occupied with the Purāṇas and other sacred texts. When the sun has set, he should bathe again according to the prescribed rites.

Then, in Vṛndāvana, one should construct a square pavilion, adorned with flowers, garlands, divine fruits such as coconuts and other auspicious ones, betel nuts, sugarcane stalks, and plantain pillars. There, one should worship the Lord of Devas, who dwells in the Ocean of Milk, with various types of offerings, songs, instrumental music, and dances. One should cause all the rhythmic measures of the Mārga style to be played, and perform dance and drama arising therefrom; one should have the song of the god Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, sung in the Vasantarāga melody.

One should worship that Garuḍa-bannered Lord with the honors due to a great king. One should satisfy the best of the twice-born and Vaiṣṇavas who are firm in their vows with offerings and sacrificial fees, with great devotion. One should accept their blessings and dedicate all of that to Viṣṇu. Then, on the full moon day, in a forest adorned with Dhātrī trees, one should satisfy the omnipresent Lord Dāmodara Viṣṇu with various kinds of food. There, the wise person should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed for the Kalpa.

Afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and then eat oneself along with one's kinsmen. This vow is highly meritorious, auspicious, and the remover of all sins; it pacifies all transgressions and destroys all calamities. It must certainly be performed by all those residing in the four stages of life (āśramas). They say this is the occasional (naimittika) duty for those following the four stages of life: the Parāka, eating at the sixth meal-time, the observance of holding the fast and breaking it, the Lakṣavarti-vrata, and likewise the Bhīṣmapañcaka.

Likewise, the vow of a hundred thousand prostrations and a hundred thousand circumambulations—these are said to be the vows for the Cāturmāsya period; this is declared to be optional (kāmya). One should not perform the crushing of colored powders during the Cāturmāsya (one should avoid it), nor should one sow Tulasī seeds; all of this has been explained to you. This fourfold set of vows must be performed constantly by all—by women or men, and by those belonging to any of the four stages of life (āśramas). Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, women, or a Śūdra, they are likewise practitioners of the vow.

"The householder, the forest-dweller, the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, and the *paramahaṃsaka*—if they abandon these four vows, they do not return from hell. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrī Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the narration of the Cāturmāsya Vow. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrī Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the narration of the Cāturmāsya Vow.

There is a transgression incurred by not performing the Cāturmāsya vow. Thus, in the *Āditya Purāṇa*, the Cāturmāsya vow is described through the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, preceded by the mention of the transgression for its non-performance. Brahmā said: "O Nārada, when Govinda has gone to sleep, one who undertakes these four vows attains the pleasure of Viṣṇu through these very observances: In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should avoid leafy vegetables; likewise, curd in Bhādrapada; milk in the month of Āśvayuja; and one should renounce pulses (dvidala) on the full moon day of Kārttika."

O Sage, whoever eats the ten kinds of vegetables in the first month has planted a thorn in the heart of Mahāviṣṇu. Roots, leaves, stalks, buds, fruits, stems, bark, flowers, and sprouts—these are remembered as the ten kinds of vegetables. Flax, Tulasī, Dhātrī, and likewise the mango fruit—these four are to be accepted, because they were consumed by Viṣṇu in ancient times. One should not eat anything else; having eaten [forbidden food], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

When the Lord has slept for a second month, all sins reside within curd; by eating that, one becomes a partaker of sin. A mortal who remains established in his vow during the third month from my sleeping shall reach the world of wine-drinkers by consuming the milk of cows, goats, buffaloes, or ewes, remaining there until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava). When the fourth month has arrived, the best of the twice-born should perform the vow, desiring the infinite fruit of his observance, avoiding grains with many seeds and those that split.

Where a seed is seen to have two parts, whether from its sprouting or from being roasted, those emaciated by the performance of vows call it "dvidala" (a split-seeded grain). They say that many grains are bound together by a single husk, and they also call them "bahubīja" (multi-seeded) because of their covering of husks and their skin-like rind. That which is entirely edible is designated as "anna" (food). That food is said to be of two kinds, according to the cause of its birth-time: that produced during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa) and likewise that produced during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).

Food produced during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is pure after the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi sacrifice; food produced during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) is pure after the forest-dwelling meal (vanabhojana) in the month of Kārtika, once Upendra—the lord of all the gods—has risen from his sleep. Having performed the forest-dwelling meal on the fourteenth or the fifth day of the month of Kārtika, one may eat everything; otherwise, however, one becomes a partaker of sin. That which has not been accepted here by the Lord who is about to sleep, the great ones emaciated by their vows declare to be unfit for consumption.

For this very reason, others say that the Purāṇa must also be accepted. He who passes the unsurpassed Cāturmāsya period without observing its vows goes to hell as a sinner until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava). Therefore, this vow must be maintained; otherwise, there is no atonement for it. O Nārada! Whatever vegetable is eaten in the first month, by that a thorn has been offered to Hari in his heart—of this there is no doubt. If curd is eaten in the second month, cow's flesh has been eaten by him.

If milk is drunk on the third day, there is no doubt that liquor has been drunk. O best of Brahmins, if a split pulse (dvidala) is eaten in the fourth month, one has effectively eaten worms until the awakening of Hari. Then, at dawn on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), having performed the rites appropriate for the time, and having worshipped the Lord Lakṣmī-Dāmodara with Tulasī leaves, one should honor a Brahmin and his family, saying: "O God of gods! O Lord of the universe! O Lakṣmī-Dāmodara! O Master!"

"Having been instructed by you during the Cāturmāsya, and having observed the fourfold vow, I shall offer an image of your form out of a desire for your grace. With this mantra, one should offer that [image], well-worshipped with *tulasī* leaves, and afterwards feed the Brāhmaṇas according to the extent of one's wealth. And so forth. Thus ends the procedure for the Cāturmāsya.

The performance of the vegetable-vow (*śākavrata*) and other observances at ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and similar ceremonies. Now, as an incidental discussion, regarding the rule that the vegetable-vow should be observed during the months of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika, Kātyāyana states: "One should not offer vegetables and the like during the ancestral rites in the months of Śuci (Jyeṣṭha) and Ūrja (Kārttika). For such vegetables being offered are said to be equal to liquor. When the ancestors, who remain present, smell the vegetables prescribed for those months, they utter a curse; failing to eat them, they depart, apprehensive of fault."

Yama also says: "If the anniversary of death (kṣayāha) should occur when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, one must not prepare vegetables and the like; otherwise, one shall go to hell. Uśanas also says: "When Acyuta has gone to sleep and the anniversary of death has arrived, one should not offer chickpeas, lentils, buffalo milk, gṛñjana, or garlic for the sake of the ancestors. On the day of the ancestors, during the morning time, and during the three days beginning with the tenth [lunar day], one should not perform shaving or oil massage; it would be equal to the drinking of liquor. Thus [it is said].

The Specific Duties of the Cāturmāsya: Now, as an incidental topic, other duties to be performed during the Cāturmāsya are described. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, Śrī Kṛṣṇa states: "During the Cāturmāsya, one should perform a hundred-thousand circumambulations (*lakṣapradakṣiṇa*). Having uttered the sins committed by oneself and being filled with remorse, one who has conquered the senses should begin on the full moon of Āṣāḍha and continue until the full moon of Kārttika. Having completed the hundred-thousand, the observer of the vow should then perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*)."

Because it is stated thus by that much [of the text]; likewise, there is also a salutation to the *lakṣa* [of prostrations] in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Ambarīṣa, where Vasiṣṭha says: "When the Cāturmāsya has arrived and Keśava has gone to sleep, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, being composed, [one should say]: 'O Puruṣottama! O Hari! By your grace, may this vow of mine consisting of a hundred thousand prostrations (*lakṣanamaskāra*) be completed without obstacle and with all its constituent parts. Having thus resolved mentally, one should conclude it on the full moon day of Kārtika."

Because it is described with its specific regulations by the passage beginning with "Having bathed in the morning," it is stated in that very same place that the vow of *dhāraṇa* (retention) and *pāraṇa* (conclusion) must also be performed: The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O son of Kuntī! I shall describe the vow of *dhāraṇa-pāraṇa*, which destroys the sin of killing kinsmen and others, and which restrains all the senses. O son of Kuntī, O king of kings! Having made a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) at the beginning of the month of Cāturmāsya, one should then perform this excellent vow starting from that time."

This is because, beginning with the words, "In the first month, likewise at the end, and also during the Cāturmāsya," the commencement and conclusion of that vow are specified. Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between the Sages and Vyāsa, it is stated that the vow of eating only at the sixth mealtime (ṣaṣṭhakāla-vrata) should be observed during the Cāturmāsya. The Sages say: "By performing which a living being is liberated," and so on, up to: "It should be performed during the Cāturmāsya; however, if one is unable, it may be done in Kārtika. One should observe the fast for three days or two nights, or even merely by means of speech."

"One should break the fast on the third night after seeing the circle of stars; when the month has thus concluded, the wise man should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana). Having observed a fast on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, he should then perform the worship of Hari at night. This is because the procedure is prescribed by such passages.

In the *Vāyupurāṇa*, within the *Māghamāhātmya*, it is stated that the *lakṣavartivrata* (the vow of a hundred thousand lamps) should be performed during the three months beginning with Kārtika: "Having begun with, 'What is the procedure for this *lakṣavartivrata*? I shall tell you,' [it continues]: 'The time is indeed the month of Kārtika, or Vaiśākha, or Māgha. This vow yields a thousandfold merit in Kārtika; therefore, this supreme vow yields ten millionfold merit in the month of Māgha.'"

For it is prescribed therein by such passages as: "Therefore, in the month of Vaiśākha, the fruit is indeed multiplied infinitely. Likewise, in the *Pañcarātrāgama*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, it is stated that the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow should be performed in the month of Kārtika: "This vow is of great merit and destroys even the most heinous sins; therefore, the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow should be performed with great effort. Having bathed according to the proper ritual on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, one should undertake this five-day vow," and so forth, as it is thus prescribed.

In this context, the time for the performance of the Viṣṇupañcaka vow is stated. Rudra said to Skanda: "If the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism, then that auspicious vow lasting for a year should be undertaken. Alternatively, one may perform it on the auspicious bright Ekādaśī of Mārgaśīrṣa; even if that day is deficient [in duration], one should still observe this vow. There are five fasts each month, according to that count."

The twice-born must perform their duties there for an entire year, during which five fasts are to be observed each month: two Ekādaśīs, two Parvas, and the Śroṇā [full moon]. Since its performance is enjoined by such rules as "it should not be performed when overlapped by the previous day" (pūrvaviddha), that vow should be commenced either in Bhādrapada or in Mārgaśīrṣa.

The application according to specific months: Now, regarding the application according to specific months, it is stated in Hemādri’s section on the gift of the Mountain of Jaggery (*guḍaparvata-dāna*): "One should give that especially on the third day of the month of Māgha, or one should cause it to be given according to the prescribed rite on the third day of Caitra. In the same work, under the heading of the gift of mountains: "O Yudhiṣṭhira, this gift should be given on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, Māgha, and Vaiśākha as well."

Likewise, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the section concerning the gift of mountain peaks (*śikhara-dāna*), its utility is demonstrated starting from: "On the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, or again of Mārgaśīrṣa, or the third day of Vaiśākha when conjoined with the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra]," and ending with: "one should cause the mountain peaks to be given. Similarly, in another Smṛti: "In the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja, the Śrāddha should be performed day after day. Likewise, in the section on Jayantī: "In the month of Bhādrapada, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight at midnight..."

"It occurs in the month of Proṣṭhapada; it is known by the name Jayantī. Likewise, Āpastamba has also stated: "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes indeed inexhaustible. One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra. Having departed from the residence at the full moon of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa during the Cāturmāsya rites, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings," and so forth.

The excellence of the solar, sidereal, and civil months in certain specific rites is stated in the *Jyotiṣārṇava*: "The solar month is prescribed for marriage and the like; the civil month is remembered for sacrifices and the like; and the lunar month is praised for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies. And it was said by Garga: "(The Anvaṣṭakī, the day before the Aṣṭakā, the Aṣṭakās, the Yugādis, the Manvādis, the Akṣayā, and the fifth [lunar day] and others are proclaimed as lunar. For monthly and annual rites, and for increases in wealth such as clothing, grain, gold, and so forth, as well as for the provision of servants and the like, the solar and civil months are used for the reckoning of months and years. Thus ends the determination of the month.

The deities of the months. Now, as a related topic, the deities of the months are described. They are mentioned in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "In the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, the deities are Keśava and the others. The deities of the four-month periods (*cāturmāsya*) are also stated in that same work: "Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Padmanābha as the third, and Dāmodara for Kārtika—these are the deities during the four-month period. He [the same source] also states the food offerings (*naivedya*) for the monthly deities: "Fresh butter, curd, milk, and likewise thickened ghee."

The four [offerings] are dear in sequence to the four forms beginning with Aniruddha; all four are dear to Nārāyaṇa, and sugar is dear to them all. Furthermore, that which is the presiding month is indeed dear to its respective form. One should not offer curd in the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), nor should one offer milk in Āśvina. In place of milk, one should offer ghee, and in place of curd, one should offer ghee or milk. However, one should always offer ghee even when milk and other substances are available. Ghee is declared to be the essence of all things and the supreme oblation for the gods. Thus it is said, and so forth.

The Determination of the Intercalary Month (Malamāsa-nirṇaya). Now, the determination of the intercalary month is undertaken. An intercalary month is a lunar month that either lacks a solar transit (saṅkrānti) or contains two solar transits. As it is stated in the Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtra: "That month in which there is no solar transit, or indeed two solar transits, should be known as an intercalary month; it shall be the thirteenth month. Likewise, in the Brahmasiddhānta: "A lunar month that lacks a solar transit is proclaimed to be an intercalary month. Its status as 'impure' (mala) is due to the excess of time.

This has been stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Those who know time declare that the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) is the impurity of time. And the excess of time is shown in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Bhārgava! When measured by the solar year, it is completed by six days according to the civil (*sāvana*) measure. O Rāma! Those [six] days and nights are said to be [the excess] in a year. At the end of the solar year, when measured by the lunar (*śaśija*) measure, eleven days are left over, O descendant of Bhṛgu!"

"In two equal years, one month is left over; that is declared to be the *adhimāsaka* (intercalary month), and it is censured in rites performed for specific desires. This is the meaning: the solar year exceeds the *sāvana* (civil) year by six days, and the *sāvana* year exceeds the lunar year by five days. Beyond that, eight solar months exceed eight lunar months by seven and a half days. Thus, when combined, there is a month less by half a day.

Thus, this [intercalary month] exceeds [the solar year] by seven and a half days; and when added together, it becomes a month less by half a day. This is what is called an *adhimāsa* (intercalary month). Furthermore, the completion of the remaining half-day occurs sixteen days after the aforementioned time. For this very reason, it is stated in the Siddhānta: "When thirty-two months and sixteen days have passed, along with four *ghaṭikās*, the intercalary month falls."

And the state of being neuter (*napuṃsakatva*) is declared in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "That month which, due to the increase of lunar days (*tithi*), lacks a solar transit (*asaṅkrānti*) and arrives at another time, is considered neuter. The state of being neuter and the state of being an intercalary month (*malimluca*) in the absence of the Sun are stated in that very same work: "Aruṇa, Sūrya, Bhānu, Tapana, Indra, Ravi, Gabhasti, Aryaman, Hiraṇyaretas, Divākara, Mitra, and Viṣṇu—these twelve Suns rise during the months beginning with Māgha."

"The intercalary month, known as *malimluca*, is devoid of the sun and is therefore sinful. For in the twelve months, the twelve Ādityas heat [the world] in their respective order; however, in the neuter intercalary month, the orb of the sun alone heats it. Thus [it is said]. Śātātapa describes its such nature due to being overrun by Rākṣasas and other beings: "The sinful one occurring within the year destroys the fruit of sacrifices; it is overrun by the Nairṛtas, Yātudhānas, and other destroyers; it is seized by the *malimluca*s (thieves) and is devoid of the sun's transit (*saṅkrānti*)."

"One should recognize the *malimluca* as despised in all ritual acts. Now, one might ask: "If an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) is accepted, how can it be said that 'a year consists of twelve months'? This is not so; for the intercalary month is included within the latter of the two months between which it appears. Thus, this single month—comprising sixty days and consisting of both a defiled and a pure portion—is not to be considered separate [from the preceding month], and there is no room for the doubt of its distinctness.

The inclusion of the Uttarāyaṇa within this is shown by Pitāmaha (Brahmā): "Sixty days constitute a month, as stated by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa; having set aside the first half, the second half is praised. Thus ends the determination of the months.

The Determination of the Void Month (*śūnyamāsa*). Now, the void month is determined. A *kṣayamāsa* (intercalary month) is also designated as a *malamāsa* (impure month). As it is said in the *Kāṭhakagṛhya*: "That month in which there is no solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), or in which there are two transits, is to be known as a *malamāsa*; it is censured in all ritual acts. This very same void month is also designated as *aṃhaspati*. As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*: "If there are two solar transits in a pure lunar month (*śuddhendumāsa*)," [it is a void month].

That month should be known as "void" (śūnya); one should not perform auspicious rites therein. Its nature is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "A month without a solar transit (asaṅkrānti) is clearly an intercalary month (adhimāsa); a month with two transits is called a 'destruction' (kṣaya) month, which occurs occasionally. This destruction occurs within the triad beginning with Kārttika and not otherwise; in that case, there will be two intercalary months within a year. The meaning is that when a destruction month occurs within the triad beginning with Kārttika, then there is one intercalary month before it and another intercalary month after it.

Such a dissolution (kṣaya) occurs only at rare intervals. The manner of its arrival is shown in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa-śāstra): when two hundred twenty-four years plus five thousand years have passed in the Kali Yuga, in the following solar year (bhānu-varṣa), on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the Sun is in Leo (siṃha). [48] Immediately after, on the new moon of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. [47] On that same day, the Sun is in Virgo (kanyā). [49] In the same year, on the new moon of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa. [36] On that very day, the Sun is in Capricorn (makara).

46. On that [lunar] year, it is the new moon of the dark fortnight of Māgha (24). On that very day, the sun is in Aquarius (23). Thus, the month of Māgha has two transits (*saṃkrānti*). On that [lunar] year, it is the new moon of the dark fortnight of Phālguna (4). And on that day, the sun is in Pisces (30). And so it is said: the month of Bhādrapada, which follows the intercalary Māgha, becomes devoid of a transit; likewise, the month of Phālguna immediately following the intercalary Māgha also becomes devoid of a transit.

And it should not be argued that this being so contradicts the scriptural statement: "The *kṣaya* [intercalary] month occurs in the triad beginning with Kārttika, and not otherwise. For it is said: "Even in the triad beginning with Kārttika, wherever it may be externally, a lunar month joined with two *saṅkrāntis* is recognized as an *aṃhaspati*. It does not become an *aṃhaspati* during the seven months beginning with Caitra; however, when it should ever occur during the five months beginning with Ūrja (Kārttika), then there shall be two intercalary months within those five beginning with Ūrja."

In that context, the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) preceding the *kṣaya-māsa* (the month of loss) is "natural" (*prākṛta*) and "pure" (*śuddha*), meaning it is fit for all ritual acts. The intercalary month following the *kṣaya-māsa*, however, is "defiled" (*malimluca*), meaning it is unfit for all ritual acts. And this [latter] is the remainder of the subsequent intercalary month. Thus says Jyotiḥpitāmaha: "A month is said by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days; having abandoned the first half, the rites should be performed in the latter."

[Objection: "But surely, when there is a *kṣayamāsa* (intercalary month), since one month is [thus] omitted, would there not be a lapse of the rites to be performed in that month? [Reply: This is not so, because even the rites to be performed in that month are ordained to be performed precisely during the *kṣayamāsa*. Thus says the *Smṛti*: "When a single month is joined by two *saṅkrāntis*, the *śrāddha* pertaining to both months is ordained to be performed in the *kṣayamāsa*. The first half-tithi belongs to the preceding month and the second half-tithi to the following; these two months, situated within the *kṣayamāsa*, are to be recognized by the wise. Thus ends the determination of the empty month (*śūnyamāsa*).

Now, the actions to be performed and those not to be performed during an intercalary month (*malimluca*) are stated. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says concerning what is to be done: "One should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month. The obligatory rites are the *agnihotra* and others; the occasional rites are those such as the offering with a water-pot (*sodakumbha*). The meaning is that one should perform these in the intercalary month. The obligatory and occasional rites are shown in the *Kālādarśa*: "The rites for an eclipse and for birth, ending with the *sapiṇḍana*, last twelve days; the *sīmanta*, the *puṃsavana*, the *śrāddha*, and these two [the *jātakarman* and *nāmakarman*]."

"The pacification of disease, when a *yoga* is unattainable, as well as *śrāddha* rites and vows, and expiation (*prāyaścitta*) according to the influence of the occasion, [are performed] both previously and subsequently. By the word "according to the influence" (*vaśāt*), it is meant that when an occasion arises during two months, one should perform [the rite] in both; however, if it occurs at the same time, one should do so in only one place. [One should perform] the annual water-pot offering (*abdodakumbha*), the *Anvādi*, the *Mahālaya*, the *Yugādi*, and so forth; the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*darśa*), the daily *śrāddha*, and the monthly *śrāddha* for those who have died prematurely (*ūna*).

The annual *śrāddha* for those who died during the months of *malimluca*; the *śrāddha* performed at previously visited holy places (*tīrthas*) and on the anniversaries of the *yugas*; whatever gift is given on the anniversaries of the *manus*, as well as daily gifts; the rites involving sesame, land, cows, and gold; the performance of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsana*); the *parva-homa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the sacrifice of one’s own fire on the festival days (*parvan*); the obligatory *agnihotra* oblation and the worship of deities and guests; bathing according to the prescribed rules, the avoidance of forbidden food and drink, and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for specific occasions—all these must be performed in both cases (in the intercalary month and the regular month) because they are obligatory. Thus it is said.

The things to be avoided are also stated in that very same place: giving that is impermanent or without a proper cause, the great sacrificial rites (mahā-ādi), the consecration of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna), the performance of sacrifices (adhvara), the first-time visit to a holy ford (apūrva-tīrthayātrā), the worship of deities (marekṣaṇa), the consecration of temples, groves, tanks, and the like, the tying of the sacred girdle (mauñjibandhana), the formal adoption of a stage of life (āśrama-svīkṛti), the optional release of a bull (kāmya-vṛṣotsarga), the departure from home (niṣkrama), the coronation of a king, the first tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma), the various vows (vrata), the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), the commencement of building houses, the entry into a new house, the ceremonial bath (snāna), marriage, the naming ceremony (nāma), and great festivals for the gods.

"One should avoid, during the *malamāsa*, the commencement and completion of vows, rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), [the giving of gifts] for the sake of the sinful, and all expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). The meaning of these terms is stated as follows: by the word "non-regular" (*anitya*), there is the exclusion of the daily prescribed giving; by the word "without cause" (*animitta*), there is the exclusion of giving prescribed for specific lunar days such as the *alabhyayoga*; the meaning is that it refers to giving for a desired object according to one's own will. The *smārta* refers to the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites; the *kāmya* refers to the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices; and *prāyaścitta* refers to all expiations, such as those lasting three years or six years. (And the commencement?)

The rites to be performed in the month of Śuddha are stated in the *Kālādarśa*: "The Upākarma and Utsarjana, the offering of the Pavitra and the Damana, the Avaroha, the Hemantāṣṭakā, the Bali-offering to the serpents, the Bali-offering to Īśāna, the recumbence of Viṣṇu, the installation and consecration of Durga and Indra, and the raising of the banner for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra)—these are proclaimed [to be performed]. They are not prohibited in the preceding [month], nor are other divine rites [prohibited] in the following. Now, it may be asked: "All rites pertaining to the Śruti and Smṛti are prescribed for the twelfth month."

However, in the thirteenth month, all those [rites] are declared to be fruitless. If it is asked, "How can this be so, given that such statements as 'Therefore, one should by no means perform them in the thirteenth month' prohibit the performance of the ritual acts themselves?"—the answer is: no, for those statements are intended to prohibit optional (kāmya) rites. And thus says the Smṛti: "One should avoid all optional rites, such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and others, during the intercalary month. Furthermore, this prohibition of optional rites concerns both their commencement and their completion.
