"Those months which are called 'sunless' (*asūryā*) are not approved by me for the commencement or completion of vows and sacrifices"—since this prohibits only the commencement and completion [of rites] during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), a desired rite that was already commenced when an intercalary month fell between the start and the end must be performed. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "When an intercalary month has fallen, this very same sequence of rules applies. In this regard, the sequence is as follows: there is no prohibition against a rite already commenced prior to the intercalary month.

"An optional rite (*kāmyakarman*) commenced prior to the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) must be completed even when the intercalary month has arrived; of this there is no doubt. This is because of such a statement. However, Hemādri maintains that this sentence is intended for those who, out of ignorance, commence an optional rite even during an intercalary month, so that if they were to complete it therein, there would be an excess of fault. In the *Mādhavīya*, however, the statement "commenced prior to the intercalary month" refers to subjects such as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *ahīna*, and *satra* sacrifices, which are initiated according to the solar month (*sāvanamāsa*).

It has been stated that there is no fault [in this], because it does not apply to all ritual actions (*sarvakarma*). That which is optional (*kāmya*) but has no other recourse must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*); such is the case with the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others. If one were to wait for a pure month for the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and so forth, there would be a loss of rain and other benefits at that time. In the same way, the *Āgneya*, *Rākṣoghna*, and other such rites should be understood. Thus, obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites that have no other recourse must also be performed in an intercalary month, but not those that have another recourse. This is because of the prohibition: "In an intercalary month, one should not perform any rite that has another recourse, whether it be obligatory or occasional."

Rites such as the *aupāsana*, *vaiśvadeva*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, and others are "eternal" (*nitya*) and have no other alternative course. They are eternal in the sense that they must necessarily be performed, because scripture declares that sin (*pratyavāya*) accrues from their non-performance. Even though a rite like the *jyotiṣṭoma* is eternal, it is indeed to be abandoned [during an intercalary month], since its performance can take place in a pure month even if it is avoided during the intercalary month. However, the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, having no other alternative course, must certainly be performed; for since one cannot subsist without old grain, its necessity remains mandatory even in the intercalary month.

But Paiṭhīnasi has stated an alternative: "In a month devoid of a *saṅkrānti*, one may perform either the *Āgrayaṇa* or the *Navā* [sacrifices]. Occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as bathing during eclipses are those for which there is no other recourse. As Yama has said: "Bathing, *śrāddha*, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), and so forth—these should be performed even in an intercalary month, whether they are obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*). Occasional rites for which there is an alternative recourse include the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others. Now, it might be argued that from the phrase "during the *Mahālaya*, the *Yugādis*, etc.," it appears that those [rites] must be performed in both [the regular and the intercalary months].

If it is argued that this is not correct because of the prohibition: "One should not perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, the Gayā-śrāddha, the Agnyādheya, the Mahālaya, the royal consecration, or rites for specific desires during the intercalary month (malimluca)," we reply: here, by the word "Mahālaya," the śrāddha of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa) is meant; they say that it is this which is prohibited by the aforementioned rule. That is incorrect, because that very śrāddha, being occasional (naimittika), is not subject to prohibition. Its status as both obligatory and occasional is stated in the Purāṇa, like the Saṃkrānti: "Those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo..."

"Whatever is given to the ancestors on those [occasions] is equal to a sacrifice and becomes inexhaustible. Thus, because it is occasional (*naimittika*), it falls within the scope of the prohibition; for the prohibition applies only to other acts, according to the rule: "Having omitted the occasional rite. Furthermore, it is specifically enjoined by such statements as: "[One should perform Śrāddha] on the New Moon, with a water-pot, on the Anvaṣṭakā days, during the Mahālaya, on the Yugādi days," and so forth. Regarding the Śrāddha on the New Moon, some say: "If there should be an intercalary month (*malimluca*) exceeding the year, one should not perform the Śrāddha on that thirteenth month when the moon has waned."

Thus, some say that the *darśa-śrāddha* should not be performed; however, that is incorrect, because that [prohibition] refers specifically to the optional (*kāmya*) *darśa-śrāddha*. For Śātātapa has stated that it must be performed even in that case: "If an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) falls within a year, one should perform the monthly rites for both months, and one should observe the *darśa* rite for both. Furthermore, a specific rule is stated in the *Yama-smṛti*: "One should perform [the monthly rites] in both months as well—[namely] during pregnancy, for a usurer, for a servant, and at the monthly *śrāddha* ceremony."

"One should not avoid the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) in the case of the obligatory *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. Regarding the *puṃsavana* rite during pregnancy, regarding usury (the matter of interest), and here specifically regarding the annual (*ābdika*) rites, a special rule is stated. Thus says Hārīta: "The *piṇḍa* rite should be performed by the twice-born every year in the twelfth month; however, it may sometimes occur in the thirteenth month, except for the very first year. In this regard, although it is said: "The annual *śrāddha* for one's mother and father should be performed on the day of their death every year..."

The *Kālādarśa* establishes that the annual *śrāddha* (sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha) should be performed on both occasions, based on such statements as: "That rite must be performed even during two months [of intercalation], according to the word of Vyāsa. Nevertheless, according to the views of Hemādri, Mādhava, Aparārka, and others, the first annual *śrāddha* is to be performed in the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), whereas the second and subsequent annual *śrāddhas* are to be performed only in the pure month (*śuddhamāsa*). Furthermore: "The first annual rite must be performed by the twice-born even in a non-saṃkrānti month; likewise, the monthly *śrāddha* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are to be performed in the same manner."

This is because of the statement of Hārīta: "That which is the first annual [śrāddha] (ābdika), one should perform it during the intercalary month (malimluca)," and also because of the Smṛti text: "If the first annual śrāddha falls upon an intercalary month, it should be performed in the twelfth month; for others, however, it is later. Furthermore, from the words of Vyāsa: "For those who died in a pure month, the first annual śrāddha occurs in the intercalary month," and from the words of Laugākṣi: "When the twelfth month is fully completed, it should be performed on the very next day"—this is the meaning of Vyāsa’s statement.

This is because of the scriptural statement: "On whichever day of a month, fortnight, or lunar date a person dies, they know that a corresponding day of the same nature every year to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death). Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement: "When the fourteenth [lunar day] arrives, one should perform the *punarābdika*. For the term *punarābdika* refers to the second annual rite and subsequent ones; the meaning is that when the thirteenth month has passed, one should perform it on the first day of the fourteenth. Thus, there is no contradiction.

As for the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "If an intercalary month (adhikamāsa) should occur when the day of the Śrāddha has arrived, one should perform the Śrāddha in both months; thus one does not err"; and as for that which Vyāsa says: "Rites for the gods are to be performed in the [succeeding] month, and rites for the ancestors in both"—these refer to the subject of monthly and other such Śrāddhas. For it is stated in the *Candrikā*: "One should perform the Śrāddha on the occasion of the solar ingress (saṅkrānti), the monthly Śrāddha, the Śrāddha of the dark fortnight, the Manvādi Śrāddha, and the Tīrtha Śrāddha, even in both months."

The *tīrtha-śrāddha* is that performed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) according to one's prior vision; Bhaṭṭa [Raghunātha], in his *Tristhalī-setu*, maintains that this should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Furthermore, as stated in the *Nirṇayāmṛta* based on the aforementioned passage from the *Kālādarśa*: "In order to avoid the fruitlessness of the day of the *śrāddha* in an intercalary month, one should feed Brahmins with the intent for the ancestors and then perform the *sapiṇḍaka-śrāddha* in the pure month. However, when there is no solar transit (*asaṅkrānta*), the *śrāddha* is without rice-balls (*piṇḍa*); when there is a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), it is joined with rice-balls."

"Every year, as well as in both months [of the intercalary period], one should perform the Śrāddha"—this is because of the statement of Vṛddha-Parāśara. However, that too is to be considered carefully, because the previously cited text refers to the intercalary month occurring prior to the [actual] Kṣaya-māsa (the month of loss). For in that case, the Śrāddha for both months is prescribed. Satyavrata states this: "When there is only one month joined by two *saṃkrāntis*, the Śrāddha pertaining to both months is recommended even in the *malamāsa*. Here, "pertaining to both months" means belonging to the previous *saṃkrānti* and belonging to the *kṣaya* [month].

Hemādri states that by the word "api" (also), the preceding intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is included along with the *malamāsa* and the *kṣayamāsa*. For those who died during a *malamāsa*, the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) must be performed whenever that very month recurs; it should never be performed for others. As Bhṛgu says: "The annual śrāddha for those who died in an intercalary month must be performed in that [subsequent] intercalary month, but never for others. A double Āṣāḍha (*dvirāṣāḍha*) is likewise merely a variety of the intercalary month.

Regarding this, Mihira says: "This which is called *dvirāṣāḍha* (double Āṣāḍha) should not be considered anything other than an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*); due to a difference in designation, that very month is said to be for the purpose of determining the reclining of Hari. He states the same thing as follows: "When two new moons (*darśa*) occur within the period from Aries to Gemini, then, in the course of the year, Hari shall necessarily sleep when the sun is in Gemini. When two new moons also occur within the period from Cancer to [the end of] the triad [of signs], then, in the course of the year, Hari shall necessarily sleep when the sun is in Cancer," and so forth.

Regarding the determination of the *Śayana-ekādaśī* in the intercalary month (*dvirāṣāḍha*), Vidyāraṇya quotes Śruti and Vṛddhamihira: "When the sun enters [its northern course] on the tenth day or later of the dark fortnight, that is to be known as *dvirāṣāḍha*; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer. Marīci also says: "If the sun moves into Aries on the tenth day or later of the dark fortnight, that is to be known as *dvirāṣāḍha*; the sun sleeps in Cancer," and so forth. Thus ends the determination of the intercalary month.

The Determination of the Fortnight (*pakṣanirṇaya*): Now the determination of the fortnight is being made. A "fortnight" (*pakṣa*) is that period in which the filling or the waning of the fifteen digits of the moon is encompassed, and so forth. Regarding this, in the *Taittirīyaka-hotṛ-brāhmaṇa*, beginning with the passage "Prajāpati desired," it says: "Those two became the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). The gods were created following the bright fortnight, and the Asuras [were created] following the dark fortnight. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras perished. For whomsoever one should desire, 'May he become more prosperous'... [and so on].

"One should cause him to perform a sacrifice during the first fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). If one desires of someone, 'May he become worse off,' one should cause him to perform a sacrifice during the latter fortnight (aparapakṣa); he indeed becomes worse off. Therefore, the first fortnight is more compassionate than the latter fortnight. "Vasīyān" means more prosperous; "pāpīyān" means destitute of wealth. It is called "kāruṇyataraḥ" (more compassionate) because, by bringing about auspicious results for the performers, it evokes compassion. Regarding its application, it is stated in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "That month, possessing two fortnights, is celebrated in this world as 'Sa-māsa' (the month)."

"The waxing phase is bright (śukla), and the waning phase is dark (asita). Beginning with the words 'The gods and the ancestors also...', it says: 'Then, having heard those words, I undertook a religious observance (niyama). There, in general, I gave the bright [fortnight] to the gods and the dark fortnight to the ancestors,' and so forth, thereby describing its application. Likewise, its application is stated in various places, such as 'on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight' and so on. Thus is the determination of the fortnights."

The Nature of the Tithi; now, the general determination of the tithis. The nature of the tithi is stated in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*: "Because they are extended by means of a *kalā*, therefore they are known as *tithis*. With this very intention, it is also said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "O fair-faced one, those sixteen *kalās* of the moon, beginning with the new moon (*amā*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), are declared to be the *tithis*."

Thus, a specific period of time is called a *tithi* because it extends (*tanoti*) either a single digit of the moon as it waxes or as it wanes; or, it is so called because it is extended by the aforementioned digit. Now, one might ask: "If there are fifteen [tithis] beginning with the first day (*pratipad*), how can there be sixteen? The answer is: fifteen are those useful for the conventional reckoning of days, characterized by their decrease and increase. But the Goddess, known as the Great Digit (*mahākalā*), is said to be the sixteenth part; she is the supreme *māyā* who sustains the bodies of embodied beings.

By this statement, it is declared that the portion of the lunar disc measuring one-sixteenth part, known as a *tithi*, is called a *kalā*. Taking those [sixteen parts], the statement "sixteen" is not contradictory. Among those *kalās*, fifteen deities beginning with Agni and ending with Prajāpati drink each *kalā* in succession. Therein, the *kalā* to be drunk by Agni is drunk first; thus it is called the "first. A specific point of time conjoined with that [first *kalā*] is denoted by the word *pratipad*, which expresses priority.

In this manner, the names of the lunar days (tithis) from the second up to the fifteenth are to be understood. These are the lunar days of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). Furthermore, those yellow digits (kalās), having emerged from the deities beginning with Agni in that same sequence, fill the lunar orb. The specific divisions of time conjoined with these digits are the lunar days belonging to the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), beginning with the first day (pratipad). The detailed account of their origin, however, is to be seen in the section on the origin of the Moon (somotpatti).

If it be objected: "In another Smṛti, beginning with the words, 'When the measurement of time occurs by means of the motion of the moon and sun, then, relying upon their motion, I shall declare the determination,' the entry and exit of the lunar digits (kalās) into the sun are set forth; however, in the account of the origin of Soma, [it is said] they enter the deities such as Fire (Agni). Therefore, there is a contradiction"—we say no. For in that context, the entry and exit of the digits may occur either into the sun or into the deities such as Fire.

Nevertheless, there is no contradiction in the fact that the lunar days (tithis), such as the first day (pratipad) and others, are indeed governed by the *kalās*. In this regard, generally speaking, a lunar day is of three kinds: *kharvā*, *darpā*, and *hiṃsrā*. A *kharvā* is an equal lunar day; a *darpā* is one joined with increase (*vṛddhi*); and a *hiṃsrā* is one joined with decrease (*kṣaya*). Each of these three types of lunar days is further twofold: complete (*sampūrṇā*) and partial (*khaṇḍā*). Among these, the complete lunar day is shown in the Skanda Purāṇa: "All [lunar days], beginning with the first (*pratipad*), [are complete] from sunrise until the next sunrise."

"Those [days] excluding the day of Hari (Harivāsara) are known as 'complete' (sampūrṇā). That which is not of such a nature is 'defective' (khaṇḍā). In this regard, since there is no doubt concerning the injunctions and prohibitions when the lunar day (tithi) is complete, the injunctions and prohibitions are applied to the defective lunar day.

In this regard, the partial lunar days (*khaṇḍatithi*) beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇimā*) are now determined. Among these, the word *pratipad* refers to the commencement. That lunar fortnight or month is called *pratipad* because it begins (*pratipadyate*) on that lunar day. When that day extends from sunrise until the next sunrise, it is considered "pure" (*śuddha*), and therefore everything prescribed for the first day should be performed without hesitation.

And purity (*śuddhatva*) is demonstrated in the *Nāradīya*: "The lunar day (*tithi*) that begins at the time of sunrise and lasts for sixty *nāḍikās* shall be pure; this rule applies to all lunar days. When that lunar day—be it the first day (*pratipad*) or others—is joined with the preceding and following days by the new moon (*darśa*) or the second day (*dvitīyā*) respectively, then it is a "fragmentary" (*khaṇḍā*) day.

In this regard, a determination is made concerning the following doubt: Should all observances, such as vows and fasts associated with the first lunar day (pratipad) and so forth, be performed when that first day is joined with the new moon (darśa), or when it is joined with the second lunar day (dvitīyā)? On this point, the vow, fast, and other observances must be performed on the first lunar day joined specifically with the new moon. This is because of the "Yugma" rule. The Yugma rule is stated in the Nigama: "For the pairs of two, three, four, and five; for six and seven; for eight and nine; the twelfth joined with the eleventh, and the full moon joined with the fourteenth. (Note: The term *yugma* refers to the pairing of lunar days; thus, the first day is paired with the new moon, the second with the first, and so on.)

"Even when the new moon occurs on the [preceding] lunar day, the pair of lunar days yields great fruit; this same [pair], when reversed, causes great harm and destroys previously accumulated merit. Here, the words beginning with "Yugma" (the pair) and ending with "Randhra" (the ninth) denote the lunar days starting from the second and third up to the ninth. "Rudra" refers to the eleventh. The meaning is that there are seven pairs: the second joined with the third, and the third joined with the second, and so forth.

By this pair of verses, the excellence of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) when it is overlapped by the preceding [new moon] is understood, because it is stated that "the new moon is also present on the first day. Regarding the specific rule for the tenth day, the *Purāṇasamuccaya* states: "The tenth day should be performed as complete, or else mixed with the preceding [ninth]. Regarding the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, Sumantu has said: "O Sage, the thirteenth day should be observed together with the twelfth. Thus, concerning the new moon and the first day, [it is said]: "The fifth, the seventh, the tenth, and the thirteenth..."

"One should perform the rite on the first lunar day (pratipad) itself when it is present [in conjunction with the previous day]"—such statements from Paiṭhīnasi and others are to be observed. In the Hemādri, it is stated that "present" (sammukhā) means the first lunar day joined with the new moon (darśa). Others hold that it refers to a day that extends into the afternoon (aparāhṇa) or the evening (sāyāhna). Regarding the statement of Āpastamba—"The first lunar day should be joined with the second; the second should be joined with the first; and the third lunar day, when joined with the fourth, yields fruit"—it should be understood that this refers specifically to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: generally, on the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), the lunar day (tithi) overlapping with the preceding one is to be accepted, while on the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), that overlapping with the following one is to be taken; however, there are exceptions. The specific details are to be understood from particular scriptural statements. As it is said: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight should be observed as overlapping with the preceding day; they should never be taken as overlapping with the following day. Regarding the nature of this overlap (vedha), Paiṭhīnasi has stated: "In both fortnights, the lunar days [overlap] with the preceding and likewise with the succeeding day."

"They pierce [the tithi] for three muhūrtas; this is remembered as the general rule. However, in the Hemādri, even two muhūrtas are mentioned: "When the sun has risen, it is for the deities (daivata); when the sun has set, it is for the ancestors (pitrya). That tithi which lasts for two muhūrtas during the three periods of the day is [valid] for both havya and kavya offerings. This state of lasting for two muhūrtas is a secondary alternative (anukalpa), according to the statement of Dakṣa: "Even that tithi which lasts for two muhūrtas must be observed if it is increasing. This piercing (vedha) occurs only in the morning.

In the evening, however, there is indeed a *vedha* (piercing) of three *muhūrtas*. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The lunar day (*tithi*) upon reaching which the sun sets, that very *tithi* is declared for that day, provided it lasts for at least three *muhūrtas*. As for those other statements from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, such as: "In the case of vows, fasts, ritual baths, and the like, even a single *ghaṭikā* [of a *tithi*] occurring at sunrise is to be accepted; however, the opposite is the rule for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*)," these are intended to praise the three-*muhūrta* duration by way of extolling its constituent *ghaṭikās* and so forth.

For this very reason, Bodhāyana states: "That lunar day which remains for three muhūrtas at sunrise is indeed the [valid] lunar day; it is recommended for ritual observances such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation. There are many such statements establishing the primacy of the three-muhūrta duration, which are not written here for fear of excessive length. In this matter, disregarding the time of three muhūrtas and so forth, the vow and other rites should be performed when the lunar day extends through the period of the ritual action and is sufficient for the performance.

This has been stated by Vyāsa: "When the time consists of only three *muhūrtas*, it is not possible to give a gift; rather, that which is sufficient for the performance [of the rite] should be accepted. This is the rule for all gifts. Likewise, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Whichever lunar day (*tithi*) pervades the specific time of a particular rite, one should perform that rite during that [pervading] time; the waning or waxing [of the moon] is not the cause [for choosing]. In the absence of such [a time], the alternative of three *muhūrtas* applies. As for the statement: "Kharva, Darpa, and Hiṃsra—these are the three characteristics of a lunar day..."

Regarding the statement of Vyāghra, "The two [tithis] characterized by deficiency and pride (Kharva and Darpa) are to be honored; Histrā belongs to the preceding time," that refers to the subject matter of *ekoddiṣṭa* and other types of *śrāddha*. This is because of the declaration in the Nigama: "In the case of the annual *śrāddha* and others, there is an injunction regarding increase and decrease [of the lunar day]," and so forth. As for the other *smṛti* text: "Whether the lunar day (*tithi*) extends through midday or not, one should perform the rites therein; decrease and increase are not the cause [for deciding the date]," that refers specifically to the *ekabhukta* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

In this context, however, if there is no overlap with the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*), one should accept only that which overlaps with the time of the ritual's commencement (*karmopakramakāla*). This is because of the statement in the *Dīpikā*: "Indeed, that lunar day (*tithi*) which extends to the time of the ritual's commencement is to be accepted, not the [rules regarding] even-numbered days and so forth. As for those statements such as: "The lunar day upon reaching which the sun rises is to be known as complete for the rites of giving and study," these texts are intended as praises for [the duration of] three *muhūrtas* and more.

In this regard, when there arises a doubt—namely, whether the prescribed acts such as fasting and giving should be performed on the previous lunar day (*pūrvatithi*) or on the day of the ritual (*karmatithi*), given that the previous day exceeds three *muhūrtas* or pervades the time of the rite (*karmakāla*)—Dakṣa states: "A wise man, having made his resolve (*saṅkalpa*) in the morning for a fast, a vow, or the like, should perform the rite on that lunar day; the waning or waxing [of the moon] is no cause [for hesitation]. It is also stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Beginning in the morning, the intelligent person should perform the *nakta-vrata* and other such observances."

"Neither in the afternoon nor at midday, for those two are recorded as times for rites dedicated to the ancestors. By the force of such statements, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) must be made precisely in the morning. Although there is the statement: "Whatever time is prescribed for a rite, that [time] existing at its commencement constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*); it does not [constitute an auxiliary] when the commencement has been abandoned," which implies that the first lunar day (*pratipad*) must necessarily be present at the time of the resolve; nevertheless, even if the first lunar day as known from the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is absent at that moment, the first lunar day established in the Smṛtis exists.

For this very reason, Devala states: "The lunar day (tithi) upon reaching which the sun sets—that tithi should be known as complete for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study. In this context, the festival of Bali (Balyutsava) should be performed on the first lunar day (pratipad) when it is joined with the preceding day (pūrvaviddhā). This is according to the Smṛti: "Śrāvaṇī, Durganavamī, likewise Durgāṣṭamī, Śivarātri, and the day of Bali—these must be observed when joined with the preceding day. Furthermore, that festival is described in the Brahmapurāṇa, the Vāmanapurāṇa, and the Bhaviṣyottarapurāṇa.

Likewise, a specific ritual to be performed therein is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa: "On the first day (pratipad) of the month of Bala, one should bathe with oil; for by my grace, Bali formerly attained the kingdom of heaven. He granted him this boon: 'Whatever man remains on the first day of the month—whether filled with joy, anger, sorrow, or happiness—he shall generally pass the entire year in that same state. Therefore, one should especially perform auspicious rites on that day."

Likewise, giving gifts to Brāhmaṇas yields great merit; one should bestow upon Brāhmaṇas garments, horses, elephants, cows, chariots with divine trappings, and various kinds of wealth. To whatever extent that best of men performs the festival with devotion during that [lunar day], to that same extent shall it flourish for him in birth after birth. Thus it is said. Regarding the specific rule for the first lunar day (pratipad): "The first lunar day of the bright fortnight is considered auspicious when it is not overlapped by the new moon (darśa)."

"If the second [lunar day] should pierce the Kṛṣṇa [fortnight], it shall consist of three muhūrtas. Jyotiḥkāśyapa also says: "In the bright fortnight, the first [lunar day] pierced by the preceding one brings auspiciousness; in the dark fortnight, it should be known as auspicious when it touches the *saṅgava* period," and so forth. Regarding the festival of Bali as well, a specific rule is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: "When the month of Kārttika has arrived, on whichever first lunar day (*pratipad*) is bright, the festival of Bali should be performed on that lunar day which is 'facing' (*sammukhā*)."

The *pratipad* of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) in the month of Kārttika should be observed as the day when the festival is present. "Present" means it must extend through the afternoon (*sāyāhna*). Garga says: "If the festival of offerings (*balyutsava*) occurs on the previous day [the *pratipad*] for three *muhūrtas*, [it is valid]. Vṛddhagarga states: "If it is impossible for the *pratipad* to be 'present'—that is, overlapped by the previous day—then the festival of offerings should be performed on that [previous] day, while gambling and other such activities should take place on the following day. Alternatively, if it is overlapped by the previous day during the *saṅgava* period, it is forbidden; it is considered [valid] only when measured by the subsequent day," and so forth. This should be understood to apply similarly to the first days (*pratipad*) at the beginning of the year and other such occasions.

In this context, if the fast on the first day of the bright fortnight (*pratipad*) and so forth cannot be observed due to some cause, then even the secondary time (*gauṇa*)—that which is overlapped by the following day (*uttaraviddhā*)—should be accepted; for the secondary time itself is superior to the total abandonment of the ritual act. Likewise, a specific rule regarding the lunar days beginning with the *pratipad* is stated in the seventeenth chapter of the Varāha Purāṇa: "Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā are the lunar days in order; these five, beginning with the *pratipad*, [occur] exactly five times each in both fortnights."

Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva—the fifth form is named Nārāyaṇa. These deities are traditionally held to be the recipients of worship on the lunar days (tithis) in their respective order. Curdled butter (navanīta), curd, milk, and solidified clarified butter (ghṛta) are, in sequence, the favorites of the four forms beginning with Aniruddha. For Nārāyaṇa, all four are preferred, as is sugar. One should always offer clarified butter, even when milk and other substances are available.

Ghee is declared to be the essence of all things and the supreme oblation for the gods. Having offered it to me and then given it to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity, one should eat it oneself along with one’s family day after day. For one who does not always have the capacity to perform this daily offering, one should nevertheless do so at least once during the Cāturmāsya period, day after day. An offering of fresh butter and other substances should be made during the five days beginning with Nandā; for he who, despite having the capacity, does not perform the offering to me, [commits a fault].
"His birth would be in vain, and even his prosperity would be fruitless. Thus has the specific rule regarding the worship of Viṣṇu been declared.

The Determination of the Time for Eating Once a Day (Ekabhukta). Now follows the determination of the time for eating once a day. In this regard, eating once a day is of three types: independent, as an auxiliary to another rite, and as a substitute for fasting. Regarding the subject of independent eating once a day, Devala states: "That which is eaten according to rule after the midpoint of the day has passed is called 'eating once a day' (ekabhukta), provided it is reduced by at least three mouthfuls. In the Skanda Purāṇa also: "That which is eaten according to rule after the midpoint of the day has passed..."

"Thus it is declared that 'eating once' (ekabhukta) should indeed take place during the day alone. Regarding this, some say that the primary time for eating once is a period of one and a half muhūrtas after midday. Others, however, maintain that the latter portion of the day divided into five parts is the primary time. In the Hemādri, it is stated that the middle portion of the day divided into three parts is "midday" (madhyāhna). Here, because the division into five parts is more authoritative than the divisions of the day into three or two parts, that [fivefold division] alone should be adopted.

Regarding the divisions and distinctions of this day, they have been established by the statements of Śātātapa, Gobhila, Śaṅkha, and others. Among these, the division into two parts is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The forenoon (pūrvāhṇa) is until the turning point [of the shadow], and the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is thereafter. With that very intent, Manu says: "And when the latter fortnight excels the former fortnight, then for the Śrāddha, the afternoon is preferred over the forenoon."

The threefold division is also shown in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The five muhūrtas following sunrise are declared to be the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa); the next five are declared to be midday (madhyāhna); and the five muhūrtas following that are declared to be the afternoon (aparāhṇa). Gobhila, however, describes a fourfold division: "The first prahara is the forenoon; the next prahara is midday; the third shall be the afternoon; and after that shall be the evening (sāyāhna)."

Vyāsa has described the fivefold division as follows: "The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration; midday shall consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise; the evening consists of three muhūrtas and is excluded from all ritual acts. Śaṅkha has shown the fifteenfold division: "Raudra, Caitra, Maitra, and likewise Ārabhaṭa; Sāvitra, Jayanta, Gāndharva, and Kutapa;"

"Rauhiṇa, Viriñca, Vijaya, Nairṛta, as well as Māhendra and Vāruṇa—these are remembered as the fifteen [muhūrtas]. Among these, because of their utility for all Śrauta and Smārta rites, a fivefold division is primary. Therefore, the latter portion of midday (the third part of the day), divided into five parts, is the principal time for Ekabhakta (eating once a day), because it occurs immediately after half the day has passed. The time prior to sunset is secondary, since it is permitted by the rule "only during the day."

This being the established rule, the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends through the primary time is to be accepted. For this very reason, the *Padma Purāṇa* states: "In the vow of eating once a day (*ekabhukta*), the lunar day should always be taken as that which extends through midday. Bodhāyana also says: "For a fast (*upavāsa*), the lunar day is that which exists at sunrise; for a night-vow (*nakta*), it is that which exists at sunset; for the vow of eating once a day, the lunar day is that which extends through midday. Regarding the phrase "extending through midday," the meaning to be determined is sixfold.

[The cases are: the [rite] occupies the midday on the preceding day alone; it occupies it on the following day alone; it occupies it on both days; it occupies a portion of it equally on both days; or it occupies a portion of it unequally on both days. Among these, in the first and second cases, the occupation of the midday itself is the determining factor. In the third case, however, that which is joined with the previous day (*pūrvaviddhā*) is to be accepted, because although the occupation of the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) is equal, the occupation of the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) is greater.

In the fourth case, although there is no overlap with the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) on either day, the previous day alone is to be accepted because there is no overlap with the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) on the following day. This same principle should be applied in the fifth case as well. In the sixth case, however, when [the tithi] extends beyond a portion of midday on the previous day, then, due to that excess and the resulting overlap with the secondary time, the previous day alone is to be accepted.

When, however, on the following day it occupies more than a portion of midday, then—even in the absence of an occupation of the secondary time (gauṇakāla)—it must be taken on that very day because of the greater occupation of the primary time (mukhyakāla). Thus concludes the determination of the independent Ekabhakta.
